18.s:
The Indian Constitution is often described as a unique blend of rigidity and flexibility. Which of the following provisions reflect this dual nature?

1. Certain constitutional amendments require a special majority in Parliament.

2. Some provisions can be amended by a simple majority, like ordinary laws.

3. Fundamental Rights can be amended without judicial review.

4. The federal structure of the Constitution cannot be altered easily.
18.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer (A.P. Tribal Welfare
18.x: Special majority (1), simple majority for some provisions (2) and the hard-to-alter federal structure (4) show the blend. Statement 3 is wrong: FR amendments are subject to judicial review (basic structure).

18.s:
The Constitution of India is often described as neither rigid nor flexible, but a blend of both. Which of the following reasons justify this statement?

1. The Indian Constitution can be amended as per the choice of the Lok Sabha.

2. Some constitutional amendments require approval from state governments.

3. Before introducing any constitutional amendment bill, the President's permission is required to check Parliament's functioning.

4. Different types of parliamentary resolutions require different types of majorities for passage.
18.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer (A.P. Tribal Welfare
18.x: Some amendments need State ratification (2) and different matters need different majorities (4). The Lok Sabha alone cannot amend (1), and no prior Presidential permission is needed (3).

18.s: Consider the following statements regarding Constitutional Amendments: (i) In Article 368, two methods of Constitutional Amendment are mentioned. (ii) Constitutional Amendment Bill can be initiated only in Lok Sabha. (iii) In case of any dispute between two Houses of Parliament on Constitutional Amendment Bill, Joint sitting of both Houses can be summoned. (iv) The President can not veto a Constitutional Amendment Bill. Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: (i) is true: Art. 368(2) has two methods. (iv) is true: the President must assent. (ii) is false because either House may initiate, and (iii) is false because there is no joint sitting.

18.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 13(4) was inserted by the 24th Amendment, 1971.
2. Article 368 itself has been amended by the 24th and the 101st Amendments.
3. The procedure for amendment of the Constitution was borrowed from Canada.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
18.x: Statement 3 is wrong: the amendment procedure was borrowed from South Africa (along with election of Rajya Sabha members). The 24th (1971) added Art. 13(4); Art. 368 was amended by the 24th and the 101st (2016, Art. 279A added to the ratification list).

3. The Indian Constitution is entirely rigid in its amending procedure.
4. As of November 2026, the latest enacted amendment is the 106th (2023).
How many of the above statements are correct?
18.x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: the Constitution is neither rigid nor flexible but a synthesis – partly rigid, partly flexible. Wheare (balance; 'quasi-federal'), Austin ('merely diverse') and the 106th (2023, women's reservation) as the latest are correct.

With reference to the procedure for Amendment of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
I. A private member of the House of the Parliament can introduce the Bill for amendment of the Constitution only after the prior permission of the President.
II. Article 368 of the Constitution of India provides for three types of amendments-simple majority, special majority and ratification of half of the States by a simple majority.
III. For amendments that require ratification of half 55. the States by a simple majority, it is not necessary that all the State Legislatures must take action on the Bill.
IV. The State Legislatures can pass a resolution requesting the Parliament to amend Article 368 in the same manner, as it could be done for the creation or abolition of Legislative Councils in the States. Which of the statement / statements given above is / are correct?
18.x: Only III is right: half the States suffice, so not every State must act. I is false (no prior permission), II is false (Art. 368 provides two types; simple majority is outside it), and IV is false (the resolution route exists only for Councils, Art. 169).

18.s: What does a special majority for amending the Constitution mean?
o: Three-fourths of the members present and voting in each House
Two-thirds of the total membership of each House
A majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting
A majority of members present and voting in a joint sitting
18.x: Special majority combines two requirements in each House: a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
18.tq: Do not substitute two-thirds of total membership or a joint sitting for the two-part constitutional formula.
xs: Special majority = a **majority of the total membership** of each House + **two-thirds of members present and voting** — option **(3)**.
It applies in **each House separately**; there is **no joint sitting** — so (4) is wrong.
**Two-thirds of total membership** (2) is the **Art. 61** type — impeachment of the President.
xa: Art. 368 type also used for removal of **SC/HC judges** (**124, 217**), **CAG (148)**, **CEC (324)**, **SEC (243K)**, approval of **National Emergency (352)**.
**Art. 249/312** type: two-thirds present and voting in the **Rajya Sabha only**.

18.x: Only two (1 and 3). Statement 2 is wrong: there is no joint sitting (Art. 108 does not apply) – if either House rejects it, the Bill fails. Statement 4 is wrong: States ratify by a simple majority.

18.s: In India, who is competent to amend Fundamental Rights of the citizens?
18.x: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights by special majority under Art. 368, subject to the basic structure (Kesavananda). Neither House alone can, and the Supreme Court only reviews.

18.x: The amending power is limited by the Constitution itself through its basic structure (Kesavananda, Minerva Mills). The Supreme Court enforces this limit but is not its source.

18.x: Minerva Mills held that the limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so an unquestioned right to amend any part is not one. FRs, judicial independence and federalism are basic features.

18.s: What was the effect of the Constitution (24th Amendment) Act, 1971 on Articles 13 and 368?

It empowered Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 13(4), excluding an Article 368 amendment from the term ‘law’ in Article 13.
It prohibited Parliament from amending Fundamental Rights and removed Article 368.

18.x: The 24th Amendment amended Articles 13 and 368, empowered Parliament to abridge or take away Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 13(4), under which an amendment made under Article 368 is not ‘law’ for Article 13.
18.tq: Test the paired effects of one amendment instead of confusing it with the later basic-structure judgments.
xs: The 24th **empowered Parliament to amend FRs** and inserted **Art. 13(4)** — option **(2)**.

Art. 13(4): an Art. 368 amendment is **not "law"** under Art. 13 — so (1) is wrong.

The case was decided on 24 April 1973 by 13 judges (the largest bench), 7:6, under CJI S.M. Sikri; it overruled Golaknath and upheld the 24th Amendment.

21.x: The basic structure theory is a product of judicial interpretation (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973); it is not written in the Constitution, a statute or the opinion of jurists.

21.s: The Objectives specified in the Preamble contain the basic structure of our Constitution. In this regard, choose the correct answer.
o: Basic structure means that which can be amended with a simple majority
Basic structure means that which cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Article 368 of the Constitution
Basic structure refers to the Directive Principles only
Basic structure refers to Fundamental Rights only
21.x: Basic structure means the features that cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Art. 368 (Kesavananda, 1973). It is not limited to the DPSPs or the FRs, and nothing in it is amendable by simple majority.

21.s: The basic structure theory of the Constitution of India implies that –
o: Certain features of the Constitution are so essential to
Fundamental rights cannot be abridged or taken away
The Constitution cannot be amended except in
The Preamble of the Constitution cannot be amended
21.x: The theory means certain features of the Constitution are so essential that they cannot be abrogated even by amendment. FRs can still be abridged, and the Preamble can be amended, subject to the basic structure.

21.s: The doctrine of 'the Basic structure of the Constitution' as a principle of Judicial Review
o: Accepts the theory of supremacy of Courts
Accepts the theory of supremacy of Legislature
Assumes the power of judging the Legislature
Is strictly in accord with the Principle of Procedure established by Law
21.x: By reviewing even constitutional amendments, the doctrine accepts the supremacy of the Constitution and of the courts (judicial supremacy 'to a limited extent'). It is not 'strictly in accord with procedure established by law' – under that principle a court only checks that the authority acted within its powers, so option D is wrong.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution:

I. The doctrine of the 'Basic Structure' has been incorporated into the Constitution of India by an Act of Parliament.

II. Presently, the Parliament under Article 368 of the Constitution of India can amend any part of the Constitution without affecting the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

III. Parliament's limited power to amend the Constitution is also an element of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

IV. The Supreme Court in the 'Kumar Padma Prasad Case' (1992) has declared that the mandate to build a 'welfare state' is an element of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: I is false (the doctrine is judge-made, not an Act). II is true (Parliament may amend any part without affecting the basic structure). III is true (limited amending power – Minerva Mills). IV is false: Kumar Padma Prasad (1992) concerned judicial independence; welfare state goes with Kesavananda/Bhim Singhji.

21.s: In case of the Indian Constitution, what does the Doctrine of Basic Structure say?
o: The order in which the Articles of the Constitution are arranged cannot be altered
Constitutional amendments by Parliament can be only on procedural matters

Constitution is foundation of the basic rights

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the basic structure doctrine:
1. It is judge-made and is not defined anywhere in the text of the Constitution.
2. The Supreme Court has laid down an exhaustive list of the basic features.
3. Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368, provided the basic structure is not damaged.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the list is not exhaustive – the Supreme Court has never fully listed the basic features and the list grows case by case. The doctrine comes from judicial interpretation (not an Act or amendment), and at present Parliament may amend any part, including FRs, without affecting the basic structure.

21.s: Which is the first case in which Supreme Court explicitly stated that Judicial Review is part of Basic Structure of the Constitution of India?

Kesavananda protected review only implicitly (31C), Raj Narain turned on free and fair elections and rule of law, and S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) followed Minerva Mills.

21.s: In which case, Supreme Court stated that Fundamental Rights cannot be amended?
21.x: Golaknath (1967) held that Parliament cannot amend (abridge) Fundamental Rights. Shankari Prasad allowed it, Kesavananda overruled Golaknath, and Minerva Mills is on the 42nd Amendment.

21.x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld the 24th Amendment and restored Parliament's power to amend FRs that Golaknath (1967) had denied, subject to the basic structure. Sajjan Singh (1965) had also allowed it before Golaknath, but the key as given by the exam is Kesavananda.

21.x: I is correct: only Parliament, by constitutional amendment, places laws in the Ninth Schedule. II is wrong: after Waman Rao (1981) and I.R. Coelho (2007), Ninth Schedule laws are open to review for damaging the basic structure.

21.x: A is correct: Parliament places laws in the Ninth Schedule by constitutional amendment. B is wrong: after I.R. Coelho (2007) such laws can be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.

21.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 31B — Laws concerning acquisition of estates and agrarian reform
Article 31A — Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule
Article 31C — Laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c)
Article 350A — Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
21.x: Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, subject to the constitutional and judicial limitations. Article 31A concerns estate acquisition and agrarian reform, Article 31B concerns Ninth Schedule laws, and Article 350B creates the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
21.tq: Check each Article against its precise subject and identify the only correctly matched pair.
xs: **Art. 31C — laws implementing Art. 39(b), (c)** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Art. 31C** saves such laws from **Arts. 14, 19**; it was inserted by the **25th Amendment, 1971**.
Option 1 is wrong: estates and agrarian reform belong to **Art. 31A**. Option 2 is wrong: the **Ninth Schedule** goes with **Art. 31B**.
xa: **Art. 31A** saves laws on acquisition of estates, agrarian reform from **Arts. 14, 19** — inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951**.
The **Ninth Schedule** was created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**.
⚠ Kesavananda struck down the part of **Art. 31C** that barred courts from questioning a law declared to give effect to DPSP.

2. It gave blanket immunity to all Ninth Schedule laws.
3. Its test looks at the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x: Coelho (nine judges) denied blanket immunity and applied the rights test based on Arts. 14, 19, 21, so statement 2 is wrong.

1. It was created by the First Amendment (1951), which also inserted Article 31C.
2. A law can be placed in it only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment.
3. It began with 13 entries; the 76th Amendment (1994) placed Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation law in it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the First Amendment (1951) created the Ninth Schedule with Arts. 31A and 31B (and added Art. 15(4) and new Art. 19(2) grounds); Art. 31C came with the 25th Amendment (1971). Entries are made only by Parliament through an amendment (Central and State laws); it started with 13 entries and now has 282.

Reason (R): In Waman Rao (1981), the Supreme Court fixed 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment, as the cut-off date.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

21.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court?
o: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
Article 31C primacy, prospective overruling and colourable legislation
Unlimited amending power, territorial nexus and harmonious construction
21.x: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines. Article 31C primacy, Article 13(4) and unlimited amending power were created through constitutional amendments, while prospective overruling originated in Golaknath.
21.tq: Eliminate sets containing a Parliament-created amendment rule or a separately identified doctrine.
xs: **Eclipse, severability and pith and substance** are all Supreme Court-made doctrines — option **(1)**.
**Art. 31C primacy** came from Parliament's **25th Amendment (1971)**; **unlimited amending power** from the **42nd Amendment**.
So options 2, 3 and 4 each mix in a **Parliament**-made rule.
xa: Other judge-made doctrines: **colourable legislation**, **harmonious construction**, **territorial nexus**.
**Prospective overruling**: Supreme Court — **Golaknath (1967)**.
**Basic structure**: Supreme Court — **Kesavananda (1973)**.

In the **2026** debate on making **voting a fundamental right**, it was argued voting should be **more than a statutory right**.

**Kuldip Nayar (2006)** also linked **free and fair elections, democracy** to basic structure.
Raj Narain struck down the **39th Amendment** clause (**Art. 329A(4)**) putting the PM's election disputes beyond courts.

Reason (R): India has a written, supreme Constitution, and laws and amendments made by Parliament are subject to judicial review by the courts.

21.x: Statement 3 is wrong: an Art. 368 amendment can add laws to the Ninth Schedule (and amend FRs or the Preamble); what it cannot do is destroy the basic structure. 22.x: Joseph Shine (2018) struck down Section 497 IPC; the BNS, in force from 1 July 2024, has no adultery offence and no Section 377 equivalent.

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

22.x: A is false: Navtej Singh Johar dealt with Section 377 of the IPC; there is no Article 377 to strike down. R is true: the Court read down Section 377 for consensual adult same-sex acts.
22.tq: Discriminate an IPC section from a constitutional Article.
n: Navtej Singh Johar decriminalized consensual same-sex acts between adults. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]

A is false: **Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** read down **Sec. 377 IPC** — ⚠ not Article 377 of the Constitution.

24.x: Constitutional government is government by fixed rules (rule of law), not by the will of persons, so 'persons may change but rules should not change'. A republic, monarchy or socialist system does not carry this meaning.

24.s: Absolute Sovereign power of the Monarch was advocated by
24.x: Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) advocated the absolute sovereign power of the monarch, since people surrender all rights to the sovereign. Locke favoured limited government and Rousseau popular sovereignty.

24.s: Who among the following is the author of the book, The Social Contract?
24.x: The Social Contract (1762) was written by Jean-Jacques Rousseau. Hobbes wrote Leviathan, Locke Two Treatises of Government.

24.s: Who among the following supports customary rights?
24.x: D.G. Ritchie is an exponent of the historical (customary) theory of rights – rights grow out of custom. Locke stands for natural rights.

24.s: The state is a necessary evil according to
24.x: Individualists see the State as a necessary evil, to be kept minimal; anarchists want it abolished, so they are not the answer.

24.s: The concept of "National rights" was emphasised by
24.x: 'National rights' is a misprint for natural rights: John Locke made the natural rights of life, liberty and property the basis of government; Dalton, Leacock and Bryce did not.

24.s: Who among the following proposed the theory of 'Civil Legitimacy'?
24.x: Unkeyed: 'civil legitimacy' is not a standard theory name. Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau all grounded the legitimacy of civil government in a social contract, and no source attributes the phrase to one of them, so no option can be fixed.

24.s: Which one of the following factors constitutes the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy?
24.x: Separation of powers, with checks and balances among legislature, executive and judiciary, is the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy. Centralisation endangers liberty; an elected government alone is not enough.

24.s: The Presidential Government operates on the Principle of
o: division of powers between Centre and States
24.x: The presidential system rests on separation of powers between executive and legislature; the parliamentary system rests on fusion. Division of powers between Centre and States is federalism.

24.s: Which organ of the government consists of elected representative of people?
24.x: The legislature (Parliament and State Legislatures) consists of the people's elected representatives. The media is not a government organ and judges are appointed.

24.s: What is the nature of separation of powers in India?
o: Implicit, not absolute, with overlapping functions creating checks and balances
Absolute, as in a pure presidential system
24.x: India has no rigid separation; it is implicit, and overlapping functions create checks and balances.
xa: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: the Constitution does **not** recognise a rigid separation of powers.
**Legislature-executive fusion** under the parliamentary system; **judiciary insulated**.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers among the **basic features**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Montesquieu, in 'The Spirit of Laws' (1748), drew mainly on the American Constitution for his theory of separation of powers.
2. Ambedkar preferred the parliamentary system because it gives priority to responsibility over stability.
3. In India the President is the nominal head and the Council of Ministers the real executive.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 1 is wrong: Montesquieu drew on the British constitution (the US Constitution came only in 1787); he held that division of powers best protects liberty. Ambedkar chose responsibility over stability, and in India the President is the nominal and the Council of Ministers the real executive.

24.s:
Assertion (A): Article 50 directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
Reason (R): Munro's Madras Regulations (1816) vested magisterial and police powers in the Collector again.

o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

24.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Art. 50 is a Directive Principle on separating the judiciary from the executive in the State's public services; Munro's 1816 Regulations, which reversed the Cornwallis separation by giving the Collector magisterial and police powers again, are a historical fact, not the reason for Art. 50.

24.s: In Indian Polity, the executive is subordinate to the-
24.x: In India the executive is subordinate to the legislature: the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)).

24.x: Collective responsibility is Art. 75(3) for the Union and Art. 164(2) for States, not 163(2).

b. Impeachment of the President

Consider the following statements:
1. Under Article 85, not more than six months may pass between two sessions of Parliament.
2. An ordinance can be issued only when the legislature is not in session.
3. An ordinance is immune from judicial review.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 3 is wrong: an ordinance is subject to judicial review and must be laid before the House. The gap between two sessions cannot exceed six months (Art. 85; Art. 174 for States), and ordinances (Arts. 123, 213) issue only when the legislature is not in session.

24.s: In which case was the 42nd Amendment's bar on judicial review struck down?
o: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
24.x: Minerva Mills struck down the bar; Raj Narain struck down the 39th Amendment's validation of the PM's election, and Golaknath predates the 42nd Amendment.
xa: Raj Narain: the legislature **cannot decide an election dispute** — a judicial function.
**I.R. Coelho**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 Apr 1973** reviewable.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers a **basic feature**.

24.x: The 76th Amendment did so; after I.R. Coelho, such post-24 April 1973 entries can be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.

**24th Amendment** overrode **Golaknath**.

Advice under Article 143 – Binding on the President

Supreme Court review of its own judgment – Article 143
24.x: The Supreme Court reviews its own judgments under Article 137; the President seeks its advice under Article 143, and that advice is not binding.

24.s: How can Parliament override a judicial judgment?
o: Changing the law or constitutional basis underlying it
A resolution of a joint sitting
24.x: Parliament can override a judgment only by changing its legal or constitutional basis, subject to the basic structure; a simple resolution cannot do it.
xa: Examples: **24th** (Golaknath), **26th** (privy purses), **77th** (Indra Sawhney).
A validating law cannot **decide the dispute itself**.
**Raj Narain** struck down the **39th Amendment**'s validation of the PM's election.

24.x: The One Nation One Election Bill is associated with amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327. Critics argue that fixed tenure may weaken collective responsibility under Articles 75 and 164.

xs: The **One Nation One Election Bill** amends **Arts. 83, 172, 327** — option **(1)**.
Critics: **fixed tenure** weakens **collective responsibility** under **Arts. 75, 164** — these are not the amended Articles.
xa: Collective responsibility: **Art. 75(3)** (Union), **Art. 164(2)** (States).
SC: **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.
Council of Ministers stays only with **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about overriding a judgment:
1. A validating law must remove the basis of the judgment.
2. A validating law may simply declare a judgment void.
3. Advice given under Article 143 is not binding on the President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: a validating law cannot simply declare a judgment void.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review rests mainly on Articles 13, 32 and 226, and a law held ultra vires is void.
2. Article 121 bars discussion in Parliament on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge except on a motion for removal.
3. Articles 122 and 212 allow courts to question proceedings of the legislature on the ground of irregular procedure.
4. Article 142 lets the Supreme Court do complete justice and fill gaps in the law.
How many of the above statements are correct?
24.x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: Arts. 122 and 212 bar courts from questioning legislative proceedings for irregular procedure. Judicial review rests on Arts. 13, 32, 226 (ultra vires law is void); Art. 121 (211 for States) protects judges' conduct from debate; Art. 142 filled the gap in Vishaka before the POSH Act.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) held that the Constitution does not recognise a rigid separation of powers.
2. In Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court held that the legislature may finally decide an election dispute itself.
3. Under I.R. Coelho (2007), Ninth Schedule entries made after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 2 is wrong: Raj Narain held that the legislature cannot decide an election dispute and struck the 39th Amendment's validation of the PM's election. Ram Jawaya Kapur rejected a rigid separation; Coelho opened post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule entries to review.

25.s:

2. The 70th Amendment (1992) added the elected members of the Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry to the electoral college.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
25.x: Statement 3 is wrong: Lok Sabha and State Assembly members are elected directly (first-past-the-post); PR-STV is used for the President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils. Members of Legislative Councils (elected or nominated) do not vote – so a CM from the Council cannot; the 70th Amendment (1992) added the Delhi and Puducherry MLAs.

25.s:
Consider the following statements about the value of votes in the Presidential election:
1. An MLA's vote value = population of the State ÷ number of elected MLAs × 1/1000.
2. Every MP's vote has the same value, which ensures parity between the Union and the States.
3. The population base is the 1971 Census, frozen by the 84th Amendment till the first Census after 2026.
4. A State with more Assembly seats always has a higher value of an MLA's vote.
How many of the above statements are correct?
25.x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: the value depends on the population–seats ratio, not the number of seats – a Puducherry MLA (16) outweighs an Arunachal MLA (8), and Kerala (152) beats Madhya Pradesh (131). An MP's vote = total value of all MLAs' votes ÷ elected MPs, the same for every MP; the 1971 base was frozen by the 42nd and then the 84th Amendment (2001).

o: He cannot return a Money Bill passed by the Parliament.

26.x: (d) is wrong: for a State Money Bill reserved by the Governor, the President may assent or withhold assent, so he can veto it. The others are right – a Money Bill cannot be returned, an amendment Bill must be signed (24th Amendment) and a re-passed ordinary Bill must be assented to.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about the President's veto:
1. The absolute veto is usually applied to private members' Bills.
2. The suspensive veto can be applied to Money Bills as well.
3. The one-time power to return a Bill can apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the suspensive veto (return once; must assent if re-passed) applies to ordinary and Financial Bills, not Money Bills. The absolute veto is used for private members' Bills and for Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent; Financial Bills of Categories I and II can be returned.

26.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The President may return a Money Bill passed by Parliament for reconsideration.
2. Since the 24th Amendment (1971), the President must give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
3. The President may withhold assent to a State Money Bill reserved for him under Article 201.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Statement 1 is wrong: a Money Bill can only be assented to or vetoed, not returned (it is introduced on his prior recommendation, so he usually assents). The 24th Amendment made assent to an amendment Bill obligatory – it cannot be rejected or returned; for a reserved State Money Bill the President may assent or withhold, so he can veto it.

26.s:
Consider the following statements comparing the veto powers of the Indian and American Presidents:
1. The Indian President has an absolute veto, which the American President does not.
2. The American President's veto can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
3. As in the USA, the Indian President must decide on a Bill within 10 days, failing which it becomes law.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Statement 3 is wrong: the 10-day rule is American; Art. 111 prescribes no time limit, which is why the Indian President has a pocket veto without limit. India has the absolute veto (the USA does not); the US qualified veto can be overridden by two-thirds of Congress – India has no qualified veto.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about State Bills:
1. The Governor has no pocket veto.
2. Under Article 201, the President declares or withholds assent to a State Bill reserved by the Governor.
3. In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor (8 April 2025), the Supreme Court treated ten Tamil Nadu Bills as deemed assented.
4. In its November 2025 opinion on a Presidential reference, the Supreme Court held that courts cannot fix timelines for the Governor or the President.
How many of the above statements are correct?
26.x: All four are correct: under Art. 200 the Governor may assent, withhold, return or reserve, but has no pocket veto; Art. 201 governs the President's decision on reserved Bills; TN v Governor (April 2025) held indefinite inaction justiciable and deemed ten Bills assented; the five-judge Art. 143 opinion (Nov 2025) said courts cannot fix timelines and there is no deemed assent.

n: The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha, which is the Upper House of the Union Parliament under Article 80. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The State Legislative Council is the Vidhan Parishad, which is the Upper House of bicameral State Legislatures under Articles 168, 169, and 171. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The constitutional basis of the Union Council of Ministers is Article 74. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The constitutional basis of the State Council of Ministers is Article 163. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The term “Council” in Indian Polity spans three distinct constitutional institutions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xa: The Council of Ministers is an **executive** body aiding and advising the **President** or the **Governor**.

32.s:

o: Other tools, such as a Short Duration discussion, are too late
The matter concerns a question of privilege
A matter has already been fully debated in Question Hour
The scheduled daily agenda has been completed
32.x: An adjournment motion is admitted only when other routes, such as a short duration discussion, would come too late. Questions of privilege cannot be raised this way.
32.tq: Recall the condition for admitting an adjournment motion.
n: An Adjournment Motion is admissible only when other tools, such as Short Duration discussions, are too late. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 82-85]

It **cannot** raise a **question of privilege**.

o: It is moved only in the Lok Sabha.

32.s:

3. The debate on it lasts not less than two hours and thirty minutes.

Consider the following statements in respect of questions asked by the Members in the Parliament of India:

n: The three primary categories of parliamentary questions are Starred Questions, Unstarred Questions, and Short Notice Questions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 85-87]

32.s: Rule ……… (of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha) does not involve a formal motion before the Parliament house, hence no voting can take place after discussion on matter under this rule.

32.s: In which year was the short-duration discussion, an Indian parliamentary innovation, introduced?
32.x: The short-duration discussion dates from 1953; it is limited to two hours and involves no vote.
xa: ⚠ **Rule 184** = discussion followed by a vote.

2. The calling attention motion was introduced in 1962.

32.x: The short-duration discussion dates from 1953 and Zero Hour (1962) is not in the Constitution; calling attention came in 1954, not 1962.

32.s: What mainly governs the day-to-day proceedings of the Lok Sabha?
o: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha

xa: **Short-duration discussion** (Rule **193**): max **2 hours**, no vote, Indian innovation of **1953**.
**Rule 184** discussion ends in a vote.

Which of the following statement/statements is/are valid regarding the office of the 'Whip'?

I. Although not mentioned in the Constitution of India, the office of the 'Whip' has however been incorporated in the Rules of the House by the 'Leaders and Chief Whips of Recognised Parties and Groups in Parliament (Facilities) Act, 1998'.

II. The role of the Chief Whip of the government party in the Lok Sabha is served by the Minister of State for Parliamentary Affairs.

32.x: Only III is valid. The office of Whip rests on convention: the 1998 Act only gives facilities and does not put it into the Rules. The government's LS Chief Whip is the Cabinet Minister of Parliamentary Affairs, and every party has its own whips.

32.x: The Whip enforces attendance and voting on party lines, and defiance can attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.

**Three-line** whip = strict voting direction.

Consider the following statements about a privilege motion:
1. It is moved when a Minister withholds facts of a case or gives distorted facts.

3. It is referred to the Committee of Privileges.
4. If adopted, it forces the Government to resign.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 2 is wrong: a privilege motion can be moved in either House. Statement 4 is wrong: it aims to censure the minister and does not force the Government to resign. It is a breach-of-privilege device referred to the Committee of Privileges.

1. The office of Whip rests on parliamentary conventions, not on the Constitution or the Rules.
2. The 1998 Act on Leaders and Chief Whips put the office of Whip into the Rules of Procedure.
3. The Government Chief Whip in the Lok Sabha is the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs.
4. A two-line whip directs members to vote strictly as the party directs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the 1998 Act only gives facilities. Statement 4 is wrong: a two-line whip is a direction to attend; the three-line whip directs members to vote strictly as the party directs (one-line is informative).

33.x: The Rajya Sabha can delay a Money Bill for at most 14 days; after that it is deemed passed by both Houses.

33.x: The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill with its recommendations within 14 days, otherwise it is deemed passed.

o: Regulation of borrowings of the government of India

Consider the followings :

33.s: Which of the following procedures will enable the adoption of a Money Bill that was once passed by the Lok Sabha but was amended by the Rajya Sabha?
o: It will go to the President
The Lok Sabha will have to pass it with 2/3rd majority

33.s: To pass a Money Bill in the Parliament which of the following is not necessary?
33.x: Approval of the Rajya Sabha is not necessary: it only recommends within 14 days and the Bill is then deemed passed by both Houses (Art. 109(5)). (The Finance Minister's approval is not a constitutional step either, but the point tested is the RS's limited role.)

33.x: Art. 109 gives the special procedure (1), a Money Bill is not introduced in the Council of States (2), the RS only recommends and cannot reject (3); the LS is not bound by RS recommendations, so 4 is wrong.

Money bills shall be introduced in Lok Sabha only

33.s: Which one of the following statements about a Money Bill is not correct?

33.x: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, so 'either House' is wrong; the Speaker is the final authority, the RS returns it in 14 days and the President cannot return it.

33.s: Regarding Money Bill, which of the following statements is not correct?
o: A bill shall be deemed to be Money Bill if it contains only provisions relating to imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax.
A money Bill has provisions for the custody of the Consolidated Fund of India or the Contingency Fund of India.
A money Bill is concerned with the appropriation of money out of the Contingency Fund of India.
A Money Bill deals with the regulation of borrowing of money or giving of any guarantee by the Government of India.
33.x: Art. 110(1) covers the custody of the CFI or Contingency Fund and appropriation out of the CFI; 'appropriation out of the Contingency Fund' is not a Money Bill matter, so (c) is not correct (UPSC key c).

33.s:
Consider the following statements about a Money Bill:
1. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, only by a minister and only on the President's recommendation.
2. The Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days, with or without recommendations.
3. The Lok Sabha is bound to accept the recommendations of the Rajya Sabha.
4. The President can return it once for reconsideration.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statement 3 is wrong: the Lok Sabha may accept or reject any RS recommendation. Statement 4 is wrong: the President may give or withhold assent to a Money Bill but cannot return it.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 110:
1. A Bill containing only provisions on the regulation of borrowing by the Government of India can be a Money Bill.
2. A Bill is a Money Bill merely because it provides for the imposition of fines or penalties.
3. A Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it provides for taxes imposed by a local body for local purposes.
How many of the above statements are correct?
33.x: Statement 2 is wrong: under Art. 110(2) fines/penalties, fees for licences or services and local-body taxes do not by themselves make a Bill a Money Bill. Borrowing and guarantees by the Government of India are Art. 110(1)(b) matters.

33.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Speaker's decision that a Bill is a Money Bill cannot be questioned in any court.
2. In Rojer Mathew (2019) the Money Bill question was referred to a 9-judge bench.
3. The Speaker endorses his certificate on a Money Bill when it is sent to the Rajya Sabha and to the President.
4. The Aadhaar Bill, 2016 was passed as a Money Bill and upheld in K.S. Puttaswamy (2018).
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
33.x: Statement 2 is wrong: in Rojer Mathew (2019) the Money Bill question went to a 7-judge bench. The Speaker's Art. 110(3) decision is final, his certificate goes with the Bill to the RS and the President, and the Aadhaar law was upheld in Puttaswamy (2018).

33.s:
Consider the following statements about the Rajya Sabha in financial matters:
1. It can discuss the Annual Financial Statement.
2. It can vote on the Demands for Grants.
3. Demands for Grants are provided for under Article 113.
4. If it does not return the Appropriation Bill within 14 days, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses.
How many of the above statements are correct?
33.x: Statement 2 is wrong: only the Lok Sabha votes on the Demands for Grants (Art. 113). The Appropriation Bill is a Money Bill (Art. 114), so if not returned in 14 days it is deemed passed in the form passed by the LS.

33.s: Under Article ___ of the Constitution, the Rajya Sabha has limited powers with respect to Money Bills.
33.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
33.x: Article 109 lays down the special procedure for Money Bills, limiting the Rajya Sabha to recommendations within 14 days; Art. 108 is the joint sitting, Art. 110 the definition, Art. 107 ordinary Bills.

33.s: The Money Bill is defined in which Article of the Constitution of India?
33.x: Article 110 defines a Money Bill. Art. 109 gives its special procedure, 111 deals with assent and 112 with the Budget.

33.s: Why can't a joint sitting of the Indian Parliament be convened for money bills?
o: Because money bills are introduced in the Rajya Sabha

Because money bills don't require approval from both houses

33.x: A joint sitting resolves deadlocks, but on a Money Bill the Lok Sabha has overriding powers – the Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days – so no deadlock arises. Money Bills start only in the LS and the RS has no equal power over them.

33.x: A Bill at a joint sitting is passed by a simple majority of the members of both Houses present and voting (Art. 108(4)); no special majority is needed.

33.s: When a bill is referred to a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament, it has to be passed by

33.x: A Bill at a joint sitting is passed by a simple majority of the members of both Houses present and voting (Art. 108(4)), not a two-thirds or three-fourths majority.

o: Council of Ministers may once again request for the Joint Sitting
Each house can again pass the bill separately
The Bill will come to an end

three-fourths majority of members present and voting
33.x: Art. 108(4): the Bill is passed by a majority of the total members of both Houses present and voting – a simple majority, not two-thirds or absolute.

33.s: Which of the following statements is/are true in reference to the joint sitting of Parliament for passage of bill? (i) Provision for joint sitting is applicable for ordinary bills, financial bills and constitutional amendment bills (ii) In no situation, Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha can preside over the joint sitting (iii) Quorum of 1/6th of the total number of members of both Houses to be maintained for joint sitting

33.s:
Consider the following statements about the grounds for a joint sitting under Article 108:
1. A joint sitting may be held if the other House rejects a Bill passed by one House.
2. In counting the six-month period, periods of prorogation or adjournment for more than 14 consecutive days are excluded.
3. Failure of the other House to return the Bill within 14 days is a ground for a joint sitting.
4. A joint sitting may be held if the Houses finally disagree on the amendments to the Bill.

33.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the excluded periods are prorogation or adjournment for more than 4 consecutive days. Statement 3 is wrong: the 14-day limit belongs to Money Bills; the third ground is six months passing without the other House passing the Bill.

33.s:
Consider the following statements about a joint sitting of the two Houses:
1. The President notifies to the Houses his intention to summon them to a joint sitting.
2. In the absence of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker, the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides.
3. Its quorum is one-tenth of the total members of both Houses.
4. A Bill is passed at a joint sitting by two-thirds of the members present and voting.
How many of the above statements are correct?
33.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the Chairman (Vice-President) never presides – after the Speaker and Deputy Speaker comes the Deputy Chairman of the RS. Statement 4 is wrong: a simple majority of members of both Houses present and voting suffices (Art. 108(4)).

33.s:

33.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the 1978 joint sitting was on the Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill, 1977. Only three joint sittings have been held: 1961 (Dowry Prohibition), 1978 and 2002 (POTA).

Pass it, amend it, reject it, or keep it pending for six months
Certify it as a Money Bill
33.x: The second House may pass, amend or reject an ordinary Bill, or keep it pending for six months, potentially creating a deadlock.
33.tq: Choose the option that lists the complete range of legislative responses rather than an exclusive power.
xs: The second House may **pass, amend, reject, or keep it pending for six months** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Only the **Speaker certifies** Money Bills, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: A deadlock leads to a **joint sitting** (**Art. 108**).
Joint sitting ground: not passed for **more than six months**, excluding prorogation/adjournment over **4 consecutive days**.
An ordinary bill may be introduced in **either House**.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Absolute veto — Indian President has no such power
Suspensive veto — Indian President may return a non-money Bill, but must assent if it is repassed
Pocket veto — Bill must be decided within ten days
Qualified veto — Indian President may override Parliament by a two-thirds majority
33.x: A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent. The Constitution does not prescribe a time limit for the pocket veto, and qualified veto is not held by the Indian President.
33.tq: Separate the four veto types by their effect and by whether the Indian President possesses them.
xs: **Suspensive veto** — the President may **return a non-money bill**, but **must assent** if it is re-passed — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (3) is wrong: **no time limit** is fixed, which is why a **pocket veto** is possible.
xa: Art. 111 options: **give assent, withhold assent, return for reconsideration**.
Re-passage may be **with or without amendment**.
A **Money Bill** cannot be returned by the President.

In connection with the lapsing of Bills, which of the following statement/statements is/are valid?

I. If the Lok Sabha has passed the Bill, but if the Bill has still not been discussed in the Rajya Sabha, then such a Bill does not lapse.

II. A Bill returned by the President for reconsideration of the Houses will not lapse. However, the Lok Sabha should not have been dissolved by the time the Bill is returned.
