**Jarawa, Onge** = **Negrito** (B.S. Guha).

111.s: Which was the first PVTG to receive habitat rights under Section 3(1)(e) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006?
111.x: The Bharia of Madhya Pradesh were the first PVTG to get habitat rights under FRA Sec. 3(1)(e). Sahariyas are the largest PVTG by population; Chenchu is on the AP-Telangana PVTG list; the Shompen are protected by the A&N Aboriginal Tribes Regulation, 1956. None of these three was the first to get habitat rights.
xs: The **Bharia** (**Madhya Pradesh**) were the first PVTG to get **habitat rights** under **FRA Sec. 3(1)(e)** — option **(3)**.
**Sahariyas** are the largest PVTG; **Chenchu** is on the AP-Telangana list; the **Shompen** are protected by the **1956** A&N Regulation.
xa: ⚠ First PVTG with habitat rights = **Bharia**.
The **Shompen** issue relates to the **Great Nicobar** project.

111.s: PM-JANMAN of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs covers how many PVTGs?
111.x: PM-JANMAN, with a ₹15,000 crore announcement, covers all 75 PVTGs.

111.s: In which year was the Primitive Tribal Group (PTG) category created?
111.x: PTGs were created in 1973 and renamed PVTGs in 2006; the Dhebar Commission sat in 1960-61.

111.s: Which State has the highest number of PVTGs?
111.x: Odisha has 13 PVTGs, the highest; AP with Telangana has 12 and Bihar 9.

111.s: How many of the 12 PVTGs of the joint list belong to residual Andhra Pradesh?
111.x: Kolam and Thoti are on the Telangana side, leaving 10 in residual Andhra Pradesh.

111.s:

111.s: The Shompen controversy over the Great Nicobar project concerns protection under:
o: The A&N (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Regulation, 1956 and habitat rights under Section 3(1)(e) of the FRA
The Sixth Schedule and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act

111.s: The Shompen are protected by the A&N (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Regulation of which year?
111.x: The Shompen of Great Nicobar are protected by the A&N (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Regulation, 1956.

111.s: When was the Criminal Tribes Act enacted for the first time?
111.x: The Criminal Tribes Act was first passed in 1871; it was amended in 1924 and repealed in 1952.

111.s: In the Indian context, the term De-notified tribes refers to:
o: tribes which were earlier classified as criminal tribes
111.x: De-notified tribes are those once 'notified' as criminal tribes under the Criminal Tribes Acts (1871); after the 1952 repeal they were 'de-notified'.

111.s: In which year was the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871 repealed, after which the communities it branded came to be called 'Denotified' tribes?
111.x: The Act was repealed on 31 August 1952 and replaced by State Habitual Offenders Acts.
xa: Repealed **31 August 1952** on the **All India Criminal Tribes Inquiry Committee (1949)** report.
Amended in **1924**.

111.s: By what was the Criminal Tribes Act replaced after its repeal in 1952?
o: The SC and ST Orders (Amendment) Act
111.x: The Act was repealed on 31 August 1952 and replaced by State Habitual Offenders Acts.

111.s: By what other name is the All India Criminal Tribes Inquiry Committee (1949) known?
111.x: The 1949 committee is the Ayyangar Committee; Renke (2008) and Idate (2017) came later.

111.s: Denotified Tribes were last counted in which Census?
111.x: DNTs were last counted in Census 1931; the RGI has agreed to enumerate them in Census 2027.

111.s: In which year was the Idate Commission on denotified, nomadic and semi-nomadic tribes set up?
111.x: The Idate Commission came in 2017, after the Renke Commission of 2008.

111.s: About how many communities did the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871 brand as 'hereditary criminals'?

113.s: What type of model did Sumner refer to his model of society?

113.s: Among the following what are the proposed three stages of socio-cultural evolution by L.H. Morgan?

113.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

113.s: Which one of the following is NOT a source of social change?
o: Migration of nomads in a particular season
Legislation such as the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955

113.s: According to the ILO (2025), what is India's social protection coverage?

113.x: Inclusive growth was the aim of the Eleventh Plan.

113.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the evolutionary or linear theory of social change?
o: Herbert Spencer explained change as a transition from mechanical to organic solidarity
Auguste Comte is associated with the theory of three stages
Durkheim explained change as a transition from mechanical to organic solidarity
L.H. Morgan is associated with the evolutionary approach

113.s: Who among the following gave the idea of 'challenge and response'?

113.s: Elliot Smith is associated with which theory of social change?

113.s: The idea of 'culture circles' was developed by which diffusionist school?

113.s: Who among the following is associated with 'sensate and ideational cultures'?

113.s: Durkheim's shift from mechanical to organic solidarity belongs to which theory of social change?

113.s: Who among the following are associated with the technological theory of social change?

113.x: The technological theory, linked with Veblen and Ogburn, holds that technology drives social change.

113.s: Who is the author of 'The Decline of the West'?
113.x: Oswald Spengler wrote 'The Decline of the West', a cyclical theory of social change.

113.s: Who among the following gave the idea of 'circulation of elites'?
113.x: Vilfredo Pareto's 'circulation of elites' is a cyclical theory of social change.

113.x: The British diffusionist school of Elliot Smith and Perry saw Egypt as the source of culture.

113.x: The three avenues of Dalit change are state policy, reform movements, and Sanskritisation or Westernisation.

113.s: The immigrant group, which has lost its previous cultural identity, becomes the host group. When culture is adopted, what is that state called?

113.s: Acculturation is the process of
113.src: APPSC Assistant B.C. Welfare Officer, Assistant Social Welfa

113.x: Adopting traits from a dominant culture through contact is acculturation. Cultural lag is a delay in adjustment, not adoption.

113.s: When members of a group believe that they are somehow superior to all members of other groups, what is that feeling called ?
113.x: Believing one's own group superior to all others is ethnocentrism. Ethnicity is shared cultural identity, and egocentrism is an individual's self-centredness.

113.s: What is the peaceful coexistence of a distinct human group in a society ?

113.s: The outlook which views one's own group as center of everything and all other groups are rated with reference to it is called

113.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officers (Grade-II) General Studies & M

Merge completely with a dominant culture

114.s: A farmer's son becoming an IAS officer is an example of which type of mobility?
114.x: A farmer's son becoming an IAS officer rises above his father's position, which is upward (vertical) mobility. Being a change across generations, it is not intragenerational, and it is not horizontal or downward.
114.tq: Ask whether the move is up, down or level, and within or across generations.
n: A farmer's son becoming an IAS officer is an example of upward mobility. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 21-24]
xs: A **farmer's son becoming an IAS officer** is the notes' example of **upward mobility** — option **(4)**.
**Vertical** mobility is **upward or downward** movement in the hierarchy; this is a rise.
**Horizontal** mobility is change with the **same status**; **intragenerational** is change **within one lifetime**.
xa: **Intergenerational** mobility = change between **parents and children**.
**Structural** mobility comes from changes in the occupational structure (e.g., **industrialisation**).
**Pitirim Sorokin** first set out **vertical and horizontal** mobility.

114.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Vertical mobility – Movement up or down the hierarchy
Horizontal mobility – Change at the same social level
Inter-generational mobility – Change between parents and children
Structural mobility – Change at the same social level
114.x: Structural mobility results from changes in the occupational structure; change at the same level is horizontal mobility.
xa: **Intra-generational** = within one person's lifetime.
**Sorokin** set out vertical and horizontal mobility.

114.s: A clerk moving to an equal-rank job in another office is an example of which type of mobility?
114.x: Moving to an equal-rank position is horizontal mobility; a labourer's son becoming an engineer is intergenerational mobility.
n: Caste is an example of ascribed status. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 50-51]
Gender is an example of ascribed status. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 50-51]
An IAS Officer is an example of achieved status. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 50-51]
A Doctor is an example of achieved status. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 50-51]
xa: Achieved status is obtained through **personal effort**: **IAS officer**, **doctor**, **scientist**.
**Intragenerational** mobility = change **within one lifetime**.
Achieved status grew with **education**, **urbanization**, **industrialization**, **reservation**, **globalization**.

114.s: Which of the following is an example of achieved status?
114.x: IAS officer, doctor and scientist are achieved statuses; caste, gender and family background are ascribed.

114.s: Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
o: Mazdoors include landless labourers working on others' land
Maliks derive their position from large proprietorship and rent
Kisans cultivate their own land with family labour
A dominant caste is defined only by its ritual rank
114.x: Dominant caste also depends on numerical strength and sizeable arable land, not ritual rank alone.
xa: Thorner's classes follow **land rights** and **type of income**.
**Mazdoors** also include **poor tenants** and **sharecroppers**.

114.s: Who first systematically set out the distinction between vertical and horizontal social mobility?
114.x: Pitirim Sorokin first set out the distinction between vertical and horizontal mobility in Social Mobility, published in 1927.
114.tq: Link the paired mobility concepts with their original theorist and work.
xs: **Pitirim Sorokin** first set out **vertical and horizontal mobility** — option **(4)**.
His book: **Social Mobility (1927)**.
xa: **Srinivas** gave **Sanskritisation**; **Thorner** agrarian classes; **Davis** functionalism.
Horizontal example: **one clerical job to another**.

114.s: In which year was Sorokin's 'Social Mobility', which first set out vertical and horizontal mobility, published?
114.x: Pitirim Sorokin's 'Social Mobility' (1927) first systematically distinguished vertical and horizontal mobility.

114.s: A labourer's son becoming an engineer is an example of which of the following?
114.x: Inter-generational mobility is a change of position between parents and children.

114.s: What is mobility caused by a change in the occupational structure itself called?
114.x: Structural mobility results from a change in the occupational structure of society.

114.s: Who among the following gave the concept of 'Kshatriyaisation'?
114.x: Kulke described Kshatriyaisation, in which groups like Marathas, Jats and Yadavs claim Kshatriya status.

114.s: What is a caste that is economically and politically powerful called?
114.x: A dominant caste is one with economic and political power; Sanskritisation, by contrast, is the copying of upper-caste practices.
n: Sanskritization is the adoption of upper-caste practices. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
A dominant caste is an economically and politically powerful caste. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]

114.s: Kshatriyaisation (Kulke) refers to martial or landholding groups claiming which status?
114.x: Kshatriyaisation refers to claims by martial or landholding groups to warrior or Kshatriya status.
xa: It brings mobility but **reproduces the hierarchy**.
**Sanskritisation** (Srinivas) is the other route of caste group mobility.

114.s: Which of the following is not the basis for social stratification?
114.src: APPSC Assistant B.C. Welfare Officer, Assistant Social Welfa
114.x: Caste, class, gender, age, race, ethnicity, education, occupation, income and power are bases of stratification; language is not.

114.s: Which of the following represents a form of differentiation rather than stratification ?
114.x: Sex is a biological difference, so it is differentiation; class, caste and gender rank people unequally, which is stratification.

114.s: 'Sex stratification' refers to the stratification between these.
114.x: Sex (gender) stratification is ranking between men and women (genders).

114.s: Evidences of Stratification According to Max Weber
114.x: Weber's three dimensions are class, status and party (power, authority), so 'class, status and authority'. Education is not one of them.

114.s: False consciousness in caste stratification is due to
o: They are hindered in awareness of their role in the system
They are hindered awareness of their demands
114.x: In the Marxian sense, false consciousness in caste means the lower castes are kept from seeing their real status (their exploitation) in the system. Option 3 says this; the options are loose translations, and the printed key was missing.

114.s: Who coined the term 'floor group'?
114.x: 'Floor group' is a translation of 'status group', a concept of Max Weber.

114.s: Social stratification is about
114.x: Social stratification is about both hierarchy (ranking) and difference (Dipankar Gupta's distinction), so 'hierarchy and difference'.

114.s: According to Melvin Tumin, which of the following is NOT a characteristic of social stratification?
o: It affects the life chances of individuals
It is social rather than biological
It is a recent phenomenon of industrial societies
114.x: Tumin regarded stratification as ancient and universal, not as a recent phenomenon limited to industrial societies.
114.tq: The extreme time claim in the option is the trap; compare it with the characteristic of being ancient.
xs: For **Tumin**, stratification is **ancient**, so "a **recent phenomenon of industrial societies**" is not a characteristic — option **(3)**.
His list: **social (not biological)**, **ancient**, **universal**, diverse in form, **consequential** (decides **life chances**).
xa: Tumin also **criticised Davis-Moore**: stratification **wastes talent** and passes inequality on.
In India, **Harappan** society showed differentiation (citadel vs lower town).

114.s: Besides class and status, which is the third dimension of stratification in Max Weber's view?
114.x: Weber's three dimensions are class, status and party; class position and market situation decide life chances.
xa: Weber saw caste as a **closed status group**.
**Status group**: people sharing a **lifestyle and social honour**.

114.s: Social stratification refers to the ranking of groups in a hierarchy based on unequal distribution of which of the following?
114.x: Social stratification is the hierarchical ranking of groups according to unequal wealth, prestige and power.
114.tq: Use the precise definition rather than selecting a related social characteristic.
xs: **Stratification** ranks groups in a hierarchy of unequal **wealth, prestige and power** — option **(1)**.
Language, religion, region or residence are not the unequal rewards in the definition.
xa: Bases: **caste, class, gender, age, race, ethnicity**.
⚠ **Language is NOT a basis** of stratification (**APPSC-GS 2019**).
**Melvin Tumin**: stratification is social, ancient, universal, diverse in form, consequential.

114.s: Which of the following is a modern basis of social stratification in India?
114.x: Political power and urbanisation are modern bases; caste, varna and tribe are traditional bases.
n: Caste is a traditional basis of social stratification in India. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 21-24]
Urbanization is a modern basis of social stratification in India. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 21-24]
Political power is a modern basis of social stratification in India. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 21-24]
Varna is a traditional basis of social stratification in India. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 21-24]

114.s: Which one of the following is NOT generally recognised as a basis of social stratification?
114.x: Caste, gender and ethnicity are recognised bases of social stratification. Language is not treated as a basis in this context.
114.tq: Find the odd term among the recognised bases of stratification.
xs: **Language** is **not** a basis of social stratification — option **(1)** (**APPSC-GS 2019**).
**Ethnicity**, **gender** and **caste** are all bases, along with class, age and race.
xa: Stratification = ranking by unequal **wealth, prestige and power**.
Caste has **vertical** (ranking by birth) and **horizontal** (separate groups) classification.
Among **Muslims**: **Ashraf, Ajlaf, Arzal**.

114.s: Tumin's description of stratification as 'consequential' means that it:
114.x: For Tumin, stratification is consequential because it decides life chances; 'universal' and 'ancient' are separate features.

114.s: Who among the following gave the functionalist theory of stratification?
114.x: Davis and Moore gave the functionalist approach; Marx the conflict, Weber the multi-dimensional and Dumont the ideological caste approach.
xa: ⚠ Davis-Moore = functionalist; **Tumin** = its critic; Weber = **class, status, party**.
Dumont's book: **Homo Hierarchicus** (purity and pollution).

114.s: According to Davis and Moore, stratification is functionally necessary because it:
o: Ensures equal rewards for all positions
Draws scarce talent into functionally important positions through higher rewards
114.x: Davis and Moore argued that unequal rewards attract scarce talent to functionally important positions.
xa: The theory dates from **1945**.
**Melvin Tumin** countered that it **wastes talent** and passes inequality to the next generation.

114.s: Who criticised functionalism by arguing that stratification wastes talent and transmits inequality to the next generation?
114.x: Melvin Tumin criticised the functionalist view, arguing that stratification can waste talent and reproduce inequality across generations.
114.tq: Link the critique to the critic rather than to the original functionalist theorists.
xs: **Melvin Tumin** argued stratification **wastes talent** and **passes inequality to the next generation** — option **(4)**.
**Thorner** classified agrarian classes; **Beteille** studied Sripuram; **Sorokin** set out vertical and horizontal mobility.
xa: Tumin critiqued the **functionalist** theory of **Davis and Moore** (**1945**).
Tumin's characteristics: social, ancient, universal, diverse, consequential.

114.s: Who among the following is associated with the conflict theory of stratification, based on ownership of the means of production?
114.x: Marx linked class to ownership of the means of production and class struggle.

114.s: In which year did Davis and Moore put forward the functionalist theory of stratification?
114.x: Davis and Moore (1945) argued that unequal rewards pull scarce talent into key posts.

114.s: Who among the following is associated with the concept of status inconsistency, holding different ranks on different dimensions?
114.x: Lenski's status inconsistency means a person ranks differently on different dimensions of stratification.

114.s: In Weber's analysis, what is a person's access to necessities and opportunities called?
114.x: Weber's life chances are access to necessities and opportunities, decided by market situation.

114.s:
Consider the following statements about the status group:
1. The concept is Max Weber's.
2. Its members share a common lifestyle.
3. Caste is an open status group.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
114.x: Weber's status group shares a lifestyle; statement 3 is wrong because caste is a closed status group.

114.s: According to the available studies, which is the most influential factor of social transformation among Dalits?
114.x: Printed key kept: studies of Dalit mobility stress collective action (movements, organisation, political mobilisation) as the main force of transformation.

114.s: Mandal Commission considered 11 indicators for determining Backwardness under the following three categories.
114.src: Social Structure, Issues and Public Policies 2016
114.x: The Mandal Commission's 11 indicators fell under social (4), economic (4) and educational (3) categories.

114.s: Which religion in Andhra served as a lubricant to the process of upward social mobility in medieval times?
114.x: In medieval Andhra, Saivism (especially Virashaivism) acted as a 'lubricant' of upward social mobility.

114.s: The demand of Marathas, Gujjars and Patels for OBC status is mainly a pursuit of which of the following?
114.x: Dominant peasant castes such as Marathas, Gujjars and Patels seek OBC status in pursuit of greater life chances.
xa: **Life chances** (**Weber**): ability to get the necessities and opportunities for a better life.
Marathas also figure in **Kshatriyaisation** claims.

114.s: According to the Economic Survey, poverty fell from 21.9 per cent in 2011-12 to what level in 2023-24?
114.x: The estimate places poverty at 2.3 per cent in 2023–24, down from 21.9 per cent in 2011–12.
xa: Key determinants of mobility per the Survey: **health, education, technology, institutions**; low mobility **entrenches historical inequality**.
India's middle class was **43.2 crore (31%)** in **2021**, projected to reach **61% by 2047**.
⚠ **31%** is the middle-class share in 2021, not a poverty figure.
**OECD**: India will have the world's **largest middle class by 2035**, overtaking **China**.

114.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025-26, low social mobility:
114.x: The Survey says low mobility entrenches historical inequality; health, education, technology and institutions drive mobility.
xa: **Intra-generational** = within one lifetime; **inter-generational** = between parents and children.

114.s: Southern backward classes demanded reservation in government jobs through which movement?
114.x: They demanded reservation through Periyar's Self-Respect Movement; reservation led to group mobility and broadened the urban middle class.
xa: **Mandal Commission**: OBCs **over 52%**.
Mandal used **11 indicators** = **4 social + 4 economic + 3 educational**.

114.s: The shift of the Ezhavas of Kerala from toddy tapping to tailoring and cottage industries is an example of which of the following?
114.x: Moving from toddy tapping to tailoring and cottage industries illustrates occupational mobility among the Ezhavas.
xa: Other routes: **education**, **reservation**, **migration and urbanisation**.
Dalit change: **state policy, reform movements, Sanskritisation/Westernisation**.

114.s: Which of the following can weaken caste identity in cities?
o: City anonymity and caste-blind public spaces
114.x: Anonymity and caste-blind public spaces can weaken caste identity, though migrants may carry caste networks and prejudices into cities.
xa: The Gen Z "**horizontal**" category cuts across vertical caste loyalties.
**Ezhavas** of Kerala show **occupational mobility** (toddy tapping → tailoring).

114.s: How many indicators did the Mandal Commission use to identify OBCs?
114.x: The Mandal Commission used 11 indicators (4 social, 4 economic, 3 educational) and put OBCs at over 52 per cent of the population.

114.s: The Telangana caste survey ranked how many castes?
114.x: The survey ranked 242 castes; 135 castes (67% of the population) scored above the State average on backwardness.
xa: It showed backward classes are **not one block**.
Mandal: OBCs **over 52%**.

114.s: Which of the following describes social stratification in Kakatiya society?
o: Entirely closed, with martial castes excluded from administration
Organised only around urban commercial occupations
Stratified but relatively open to mobility
114.x: Kakatiya society was stratified but relatively open; Velamas, Kammas and Reddys served in the military and local administration.
xa: **Kshatriyaisation** (term of **Kulke**): martial/landholding groups claim **Kshatriya** status.
**Sanskritisation** (**M.N. Srinivas**): lower castes copy rituals and lifestyle of higher castes.
**Dominant caste** (Srinivas): numerical strength + sizeable **arable land** + fairly high ritual rank.
The **Varna system** crystallised in the **Later Vedic period**; Harappan society showed differentiation but **no rigid caste**.

114.s: The Telangana caste survey found how many castes above average backwardness?
114.x: Of 242 castes ranked, 135 (67%) were above average backwardness.

114.s: Which of the following is NOT listed by the Economic Survey 2025-26 as a driver of social mobility?
114.x: The ES 2025-26 names health, education, technology and institutions as drivers of mobility; land inheritance is not one.

114.s: Virashaivism in medieval Andhra is described as a 'lubricant' of which process?
114.x: Virashaivism (a Saiva movement) helped castes in medieval Andhra rise, so it is called a lubricant of upward social mobility.

114.s: In which society of medieval Andhra were Velamas, Kammas and Reddys able to rise, making stratification relatively open?
114.x: Kakatiya society was relatively open, letting Velamas, Kammas and Reddys rise.

114.s: According to the Mandal Commission, what share of India's population were OBCs?
114.x: The Mandal Commission estimated OBCs at over 52% of the population.

114.s: The 11 indicators used by the Mandal Commission to identify OBCs were made up of how many social, economic and educational indicators respectively?
114.x: Mandal used 11 indicators: 4 social, 4 economic and 3 educational.

114.s: The term "dominant caste" is used to describe this.
o: Rural and urban way of life
114.x: Srinivas's 'dominant caste' describes stratification and power in rural India (village studies), not urban or tribal life.

114.s: On what basis are Daniel Thorner's agrarian classes mainly differentiated?
o: Nature of land rights and type of income
114.x: Thorner’s classification is based on the nature of land rights and the type of income derived from agriculture.
114.tq: Select the structural economic basis rather than a cultural basis of classification.
xs: **Thorner**'s agrarian classes follow the **nature of land rights** and **type of income** — option **(4)**.
They are **Maliks**, **Kisans** and **Mazdoors**.
xa: ⚠ **Maliks** = landlords on rent; **Kisans** = own-and-cultivate; **Mazdoors** = landless.
Source: **UPSC** Post-Independence notes p.**91**.

114.s: In Daniel Thorner's scheme, what are landlords who live on rent called?
114.x: Thorner's Maliks live on rent; Kisans own land and use family labour; Mazdoors are tenants, sharecroppers and landless labourers.

114.s: Which of the following pairs (Thorner's class – description) is correctly matched?
o: Kisans – own land, work with family labour
114.x: Kisans own land and use family labour; Maliks are rent-receiving landlords and Mazdoors are tenants, sharecroppers and the landless.

114.s: Which one of the following pairs regarding definitions of the Indian middle class is correctly matched?
o: World Bank — ₹2-10 lakh a year (2001-02 prices)
114.x: PRICE defines the middle class as households earning ₹5-30 lakh a year. The World Bank uses $10-50 per capita per day (PPP) and NCAER uses ₹2-10 lakh a year at 2001-02 prices, so A and B swap the two. The OECD is cited only for projecting India's middle class as the world's largest by 2035, not for an income band.
114.tq: WB = dollars/day; NCAER 2-10 lakh; PRICE 5-30 lakh.
xs: **PRICE** defines the middle class as **₹5-30 lakh a year** — option **(3)**.
**World Bank** = **$10-50** per capita per day (PPP); **NCAER** = **₹2-10 lakh** a year (**2001-02** prices) — options (1) and (2) swap them.
The **OECD** is cited only for the "largest middle class by **2035**" projection.
xa: There is **no single definition** of the middle class.

114.s: India's middle class is projected to reach what share of the population by 2047?
114.x: India's middle class was about 43.2 crore (31%) in 2021 and is projected to reach 61% by 2047.
xa: Definitions: **World Bank** $10-50/day (PPP); **NCAER** ₹2-10 lakh; **PRICE** ₹5-30 lakh.
It emerged from **English education** after **Macaulay's Minute (1835)**.

114.s: The emergence of the English-educated middle class in India is most directly associated with which of the following?
114.x: Macaulay's Minute of 1835 promoted English education, which contributed to the emergence of an English-educated middle class that later participated in the freedom struggle.
114.tq: Identify the historical document directly associated with the emergence of the class.
xs: **Macaulay's Minute** (**1835**) spread **English education**, producing the English-educated middle class — option **(1)**.
That middle class **led the freedom struggle**.
xa: Middle class size: **43.2 crore (31%)** in **2021**; projected **61% by 2047**.
Occupational base: **salaried professionals**, white-collar and service jobs, business.

114.s: Who analysed the English-educated middle class that arose after Macaulay's Minute (1835) in 'Social Background of Indian Nationalism'?
114.x: A.R. Desai traced the English-educated middle class to Macaulay's Minute of 1835.

114.s: By which year, according to the OECD, will India have the world's largest middle class?
114.x: The OECD projects India's middle class to be the world's largest by 2035; 2047 is the year it is projected to reach 61%.

114.s: What share of India's population was middle class in 2021?
114.x: India's middle class was 43.2 crore, or 31% of the population, in 2021; it is projected to reach 61% by 2047.

114.s: How large was India's middle class in 2021?
114.x: India's middle class was 43.2 crore (31%) in 2021, expected to reach 61% by 2047.

114.s: What daily income range (PPP) does the World Bank use to define the middle class?
114.x: The World Bank defines the middle class as earning $10-50 a day (PPP).

115.s: Who scientifically studied 'Jajmani' in India?
115.x: William Wiser (The Hindu Jajmani System, 1936; Behind Mud Walls with Charlotte Wiser) first studied jajmani scientifically, in a UP village.

115.s: In India 'Rythu' (Peasant) means
o: Own land and cultivate it with hired labour
Own land and cultivate it with the labor of family members.
Those who use traditional farming practices
115.x: A peasant (rythu, kisan) owns or holds land and cultivates it mainly with family labour – Thorner's 'kisan'; one who cultivates through hired labour is a landlord-farmer (malik) (printed key: A).

115.s: The exchange of goods or services under the Jajmani system takes place accordingly.
115.x: Under jajmani, goods and services pass between hereditary patron (jajman) and service (kamin) castes by custom and tradition, not by law or market value.

115.s: The system of caste conversion is an example of what?
115.x: The stem is garbled ('caste conversion'); the options mix Polanyi's forms of exchange with 'antagonism', and caste-based exchange is read by some as reciprocity and by others as redistribution, so no option can be settled.

115.s: What is the difference between an agricultural society and an industrial society?
115.x: Agricultural and industrial societies differ in their basic premises, method of production and social dynamics – so all of the above.

115.s:
Which of the following are the characteristics of Jajmani system?

A. Functional reciprocity in caste matters

B. Mahalwari system

C. Village social structure
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
115.x: Jajmani is functional reciprocity between castes within the village social structure (A, C); the Mahalwari system is a British land-revenue settlement, not a jajmani feature (printed: no key).

115.s: Which of the following is not a characteristic of Jajmani system?
o: Payments in the form of inheritance
115.x: The jajmani system rests on hereditary, long-lasting patron-client ties with payments in kind; money payment is not its characteristic. (Moved to rural society.)

115.s: Rural sociology is a field associated with:
115.src: APPSC Group-III Mains Panchayat Secretary (Grade-IV) Paper-I
115.at: Study of social structure and conflict in rural areas
115.x: Rural sociology is the study of rural society – its social structure, institutions, change and conflict in villages.

115.s: Who among the following has/have argued that the notion of 'self-sufficiency' of Indian villages is a myth?
o: S.C. Dube and Mc Kim Marriott
115.x: M.N. Srinivas and A.M. Shah ('The Myth of the Self-Sufficiency of the Indian Village', 1960) showed villages depended on outside markets; Srinivas debunked villages as unchanging, self-sufficient 'little republics'.

115.s: Who among the following termed village community as a small community ?
115.x: Robert Redfield called the village a 'little community' (The Little Community, 1955). Tonnies gave Gemeinschaft-Gesellschaft and Maine wrote on 'village communities'.

115.s: Robert Redfield while defining little community talks about four characteristics. Three of them aredistinctiveness, smallness, and self-sufficiency. Which one is the fourth?
115.x: Redfield's little community has four traits: distinctiveness, smallness, homogeneity and self-sufficiency. Heterogeneity is an urban trait.

115.s: Who stated that 'the village was not merely a place where people lived, it had a design in which were reflected the basic values of Indian civilization'?
115.x: Andre Beteille (1980) wrote that the village was not merely a place where people lived but had a design reflecting the basic values of Indian civilisation.

115.s: Who argued for systematic study of village communities, for better planning purposes?
115.x: S.C. Dube (Indian Village, 1955; India's Changing Villages, 1958) argued for systematic village studies to aid community-development planning; his Shamirpet study was a laboratory for rural development programmes.

115.s: Which one of the following is NOT an element of a rural community?
115.x: The elements of a rural community are territory, we-feeling (community sentiment), relative self-sufficiency, small size and homogeneity. Cultural diversity is not an element (UPPSC 2021); a rural community is marked by homogeneity, while diversity and heterogeneity are urban traits.
115.tq: Rural = homogeneous, so diversity is the odd one out.
xs: **Cultural diversity** is NOT an element of a rural community — so option **(3)** is correct (**UPPSC 2021**).
Elements are **territory, we-feeling (community sentiment), relative self-sufficiency**, small size and **homogeneity**.
Diversity/**heterogeneity** is a trait of the town or city.
xa: Urban life features: **competition, impersonal relationships, loss of humanistic values**, anonymity, weak social control.
⚠ **Informal ties** are NOT an urban feature (JPSC 2021).
**Metcalfe** called villages "**little republics**" — self-reliant units.

115.s: Who described Indian villages as ‘little republics’?
115.x: Charles Metcalfe described Indian villages as ‘little republics’, referring to their character as relatively self-reliant units.
115.tq: Test the thinker associated with a distinctive description.
xs: **Charles Metcalfe** called Indian villages "**little republics**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
He saw them as **self-reliant units** (asked as "**Village republics**", MPPSC 2020).
**Louis Wirth** wrote on **urbanism**; **Robert Redfield** gave the **Little Community** and folk-urban continuum; **M.N. Srinivas** studied **Rampura**.
xa: ⚠ **Redfield** = folk-urban continuum + Little Community; **Wirth** = urbanism; **Metcalfe** = little republics.
Elements of a rural community: **territory, we-feeling, relative self-sufficiency**, small size, homogeneity.
**Milton Singer** studied Hinduism in urban **Madras** — continuity between tradition and modernity.

115.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
115.x: Rampura in Mysore was studied by M.N. Srinivas. Shamirpet was associated with S.C. Dube, Sripuram with Andre Beteille, and Kishan Garhi with McKim Marriott.
115.tq: Start with the sure village–scholar pair and eliminate swapped associations.
xs: **Rampura** (Mysore, Karnataka) was studied by **M.N. Srinivas** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Shamirpet** was studied by **S.C. Dube**, not Beteille.
**Sripuram** (Thanjavur) was studied by **Andre Beteille**, not Marriott; **Kishan Garhi** by **McKim Marriott**, not Dube.
xa: Srinivas wrote **The Remembered Village** and gave the concept of **dominant caste**.
**Senapur** (Jaunpur, UP) = **Morris Opler and R.D. Singh**; also **Bernard Cohn**.
Beteille's Sripuram study = **Caste, Class and Power**; Marriott's = **Village India**.
S.C. Dube's Shamirpet study = **Indian Village (1955)**.

115.s: Who studied Shamirpet, near Hyderabad?
115.x: S.C. Dube studied Shamirpet in 'Indian Village' (1955); Srinivas studied Rampura.

115.s: Who is the author of 'The Remembered Village', on Rampura in Mysore?

117.x: T.K. Oommen identified six dimensions of communalism, ranging from assimilationist to secessionist.

⚠ **Separatist** = state **within** India (Gorkhaland, Bodoland); **secessionist** = state **outside** India (Khalistan).
⚠ **Bipan Chandra** = three stages, not six dimensions.

117.s: Which scholar, in 'Modern Islam in India', treated each religious group as the basic social, political and economic unit?
117.x: W.C. Smith, in Modern Islam in India, saw each religious group as the basic unit and stressed antagonism between such groups.
117.tq: one-liner

117.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Bipan Chandra gave three stages of communalism.
2. T.K. Oommen identified six dimensions of communalism.
3. W.C. Smith wrote 'Modern Islam in India'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
117.x: All three are correct: Bipan Chandra gave three stages, Oommen six dimensions, and W.C. Smith wrote 'Modern Islam in India'.

117.s: According to Bipan Chandra, which is the final stage of communalism?
117.x: Bipan Chandra's sequence is communal nationalism, liberal communalism and then extreme communalism.
xa: Stage 1: common **secular** interests, still nationalist.
Stage 2: interests **different** but reconcilable within one nation.
Stage 3: **mutually antagonistic** — politics of **fear, hatred and violence**.
After the **1937** elections the Muslim League turned to extreme communalism.

117.s: In Bipan Chandra's scheme, which stage sees the interests of communities as different but reconcilable within one nation?
117.x: In liberal communalism, interests are different but reconcilable within one nation; 'mutually antagonistic' interests mark extreme communalism.
xa: Extreme communalism = politics of **fear, hatred and violence**.
Muslim League turned extreme after the **1937** elections; echoed by **Hindu Mahasabha** and **RSS**.
⚠ **Bipan Chandra** = three stages; **Oommen** = six dimensions.

117.s: After the elections of 1937, on what was the Muslim League's turn towards extreme communalism mainly based?
o: cooperation with the Congress on joint electorates
117.x: After the 1937 elections, the Muslim League adopted extreme communalism based on fear, hatred and violence. This approach was echoed by the Hindu Mahasabha and the RSS.
117.tq: Link the political turning point with its stated ideological characteristics.
xs: After the **1937** elections the Muslim League turned to extreme communalism "based on **fear, hatred and violence**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was echoed by the **Hindu Mahasabha and RSS**.
xa: Extreme communalism sees interests as **mutually antagonistic** (Bipan Chandra's stage 3).
**Lahore ("Pakistan") Resolution** followed on **24 Mar 1940**.
**Allama Iqbal** proposed a consolidated Muslim state in **1930**.

117.s: In which year was the first census that recorded caste and religion, contributing to communal consciousness, conducted?
117.x: The recording of caste and religion in the first census of 1871-72 is identified as a historical or colonial factor contributing to communalism.
117.tq: Retain the exact census range and reject nearby-looking dates.
xs: Caste and religion were recorded in the **first census (1871-72)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is listed among the **historical/colonial** causes of communalism.
xa: Other colonial causes: British **divide and rule**, **separate electorates**, **revivalist movements**.
**1909** Act = first legal separate electorate.
**1905 Partition of Bengal**: Muslim-majority East, Hindu-majority West.

117.s: In the 1920s, which pair of movements represented contrasting mobilisation efforts among Hindus and Muslims respectively?
o: Swadeshi and Home Rule; Khilafat and Non-Cooperation
Shuddhi and Sangathan; Tabligh and Tanzim
Tabligh and Tanzim; Shuddhi and Sangathan
Brahmo and Arya Samaj; Aligarh and Deoband
117.x: The Arya Samaj promoted Shuddhi and Sangathan, while Muslim organisations promoted Tabligh and Tanzim in the 1920s.
117.tq: Discriminate between similarly placed religious mobilisation movements by community association.
xs: **Shuddhi and Sangathan** (Arya Samaj, Hindu) vs **Tabligh and Tanzim** (Muslim) — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses the two.
xa: ⚠ **Shuddhi and Sangathan** = Arya Samaj; **Tabligh and Tanzim** = Muslim.
**Hindu Mahasabha** founded **1915** (Maharaja of **Kasim Bazar**).
Revivalist movements are a **historical/colonial** cause.

117.s: Poverty is classified as which type of cause of communalism?
117.x: Poverty is an economic cause; separate electorates are historical/colonial, vote-bank politics political and delayed justice legal-administrative.

117.s: Fake news and hate messages on social media fall under which type of cause of communalism?
117.x: Fake news and hate messages, and media amplifying communal narratives, are social/media causes.
117.tq: one-liner

117.s: Who is known as the “Father of the Communal Electorate” in British India?
117.x: Lord Minto is known as the Father of the Communal Electorate because the reforms associated with him introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
117.tq: Use the person–policy association and distinguish Minto from other Viceroys.
xs: **Lord Minto** is the "**Father of the Communal Electorate**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
He received the **Simla Deputation (1906)** demanding separate electorates; the **1909** Act gave the first legal separate electorate.
xa: ⚠ Ideological father of the two-nation theory = **Syed Ahmad Khan**.
**Ramsay MacDonald** gave the **Communal Award (1932)**.
**Lord Dufferin** used Syed Ahmad Khan in **1887** to keep Muslims from Congress.

117.s: Who among the following were associated with the founding of the All-India Muslim League at Dacca in 1906?
o: Aga Khan and Nawab Salimullah of Dacca
117.x: The Muslim League was founded at Dacca under the leadership of Aga Khan and Nawab Salimullah of Dacca.
117.tq: Use the founder–organisation association rather than the later reform association.
xs: The Muslim League was founded under the **Aga Khan and Nawab Salimullah of Dacca** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Minto** received the Simla Deputation; he did not found the League.
xa: The **Aga Khan** led the **Simla Deputation** (Oct 1906).
Lord **Minto** = "**Father of the Communal Electorate**".
⚠ **1906** = Muslim League; **1909** = first legal separate electorate.

117.s: When did the Simla Deputation to Lord Minto, which preceded the formation of the Muslim League, take place?
117.x: The Simla Deputation to Minto took place in October 1906, before the Muslim League was founded later in 1906.
117.tq: Separate closely related events by their month and year.
xs: The **Simla Deputation** to **Lord Minto** was in **October 1906** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Led by the **Aga Khan**, it demanded **separate electorates**.
xa: The **Muslim League** was founded later in **1906** at **Dacca**.
**1905**: Partition of Bengal; **1909** Act: first legal separate electorate.
Minto = "**Father of the Communal Electorate**".

117.s: Where was the Poona Pact of 1932 concluded between Mahatma Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar?
117.x: The Poona Pact was concluded in 1932 between Gandhi and Ambedkar at Yerwada Jail.
117.tq: Distinguish the exact venue from other locations associated with the freedom movement.
xs: The **Poona Pact (1932)** between **Gandhi and Ambedkar** was concluded at **Yerwada Jail** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It replaced Dalit separate electorates with **reserved seats in joint electorates** (**71 → 148**).
xa: It followed the **Communal Award** (**16 Aug 1932**) of **Ramsay MacDonald**.
The Award was based on the **Lothian Committee**.
⚠ Communal Award separate electorates were for **20 years**.

117.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: 1932 — Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award
1930 — Allama Iqbal proposed a consolidated Muslim state
117.x: A is the wrongly matched pair: Jinnah issued his Fourteen Points in 1929 in reply to the Nehru Report (1928); 1940 is the year of the Lahore ('Pakistan') Resolution (24 March 1940). The Communal Award (1932, Ramsay MacDonald) and Iqbal's 1930 proposal for a consolidated Muslim state are correctly dated.
117.tq: Check the person-event-year combination and identify the swapped event.
xs: **1940 — Jinnah's Fourteen Points** is wrongly matched — so option **(1)** is correct.
**1940** is the year of the **Lahore ("Pakistan") Resolution** (**24 Mar 1940**); Jinnah's **Fourteen Points** were a reply, not a 1940 event.
Correct pairs: **1932** — Ramsay MacDonald's **Communal Award**; **1930** — **Allama Iqbal**'s consolidated Muslim state.
xa: **Poona Pact** was also in **1932** (Yerwada Jail).
**Hindu Mahasabha** founded in **1915**.
⚠ "Father of the Communal Electorate" = **Lord Minto**.

117.s: On which date was the Lahore or Pakistan Resolution of the Muslim League adopted?
117.x: The Lahore, also called Pakistan, Resolution of the Muslim League was moved on 23 March and adopted on 24 March 1940; 23 March 1956 is when Pakistan became a republic.
117.tq: Distinguish the exact date of the resolution from nearby dates associated with other events.
xs: The **Lahore ("Pakistan") Resolution** was adopted on **24 March 1940** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**16 August 1932** is the date of the **Communal Award**.
xa: After the **1937** elections the League turned to **extreme communalism**.
**Allama Iqbal** proposed a consolidated Muslim state in **1930**.
Syed Ahmad Khan = **ideological father** of the two-nation theory.

117.s: In which year was the first legal separate electorate introduced in India?
117.x: The 1909 Act introduced the first legal separate electorate; 1906 saw the first communal party, the Muslim League.

117.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Syed Ahmad Khan – Ideological basis of the Two-Nation Theory
117.x: Ramsay MacDonald is associated with the Communal Award; the Fourteen Points were Jinnah's.
xa: **Lord Minto** = Father of the Communal Electorate.
**Aga Khan** led the **Simla Deputation (1906)**.
**Lord Dufferin** used Syed Ahmad Khan in **1887**.

117.s: Under whose aegis was the All India Hindu Mahasabha founded in 1915?
117.x: The Hindu Mahasabha was founded in 1915 under the Maharaja of Kasim Bazar and was associated with Madan Mohan Malaviya; Salimullah and the Aga Khan were linked to the Muslim League.
117.tq: one-liner

117.s: In 1887, which Viceroy used Syed Ahmad Khan to keep Muslims away from the Congress?
117.x: Lord Dufferin did so in 1887; Lord Minto, 'Father of the Communal Electorate', came later with the 1906 deputation and 1909 Act.
117.tq: one-liner

117.s: Which of the following pairs (year – event) is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: 1930 – Iqbal's proposal of a consolidated Muslim state
117.x: The Muslim League was founded in 1906 at Dacca; 1915 is the founding of the Hindu Mahasabha.
117.tq: match

117.s: Which Act gave Muslims a separate electorate for the first time, introducing communalism into Indian politics under Lord Minto?
117.x: The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) gave the first legal separate electorate for Muslims; hence Minto is called the father of the communal electorate.

117.s: Which pact, by which the Congress accepted separate electorates and weightage, is said to have legitimised communal politics?
117.x: The Lucknow Pact (1916) gave short-term Hindu-Muslim unity, but by accepting separate electorates it legitimised communal politics.

117.s: With which leader is the All India Hindu Mahasabha, founded in 1915, associated?
117.x: The Hindu Mahasabha was founded in 1915 under the Maharaja of Kasim Bazar and is associated with Madan Mohan Malaviya.

117.s: Which was the first communal party in India?
117.x: The Muslim League, founded at Dacca in 1906, was the first communal party; the Hindu Mahasabha came in 1915.

117.s: In T.K. Oommen's classification, the Khalistan demand is an example of which dimension of communalism?
117.x: Khalistan seeks an independent state outside India, which is secessionist; separatists (Gorkhaland, Bodoland) seek a state within India.

117.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Welfarist communalism — using religion for votes
Retaliatory communalism — attempts to harm members of other communities
Separatist communalism — keeping away from politics
Retreatist communalism — seeking an independent state outside India
117.x: B is right: retaliatory communalism attempts to harm members of other communities (riots, revenge cycles). A is wrong: welfarist communalism works for one community's welfare; using religion for votes is political communalism. C is wrong: keeping away from politics is retreatist. D is wrong: seeking an independent state outside India is secessionist.
117.tq: Use the wrong-person/wrong-definition trap by distinguishing closely related dimensions.
xs: **Retaliatory communalism — attempts to harm members of other communities** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Using religion for votes is **political** communalism, not welfarist.
Keeping away from politics is **retreatist**; an independent state outside India is **secessionist**.
xa: **Welfarist** = welfare of one community only (Christian or Parsi associations).
**Retreatist** example: **Bahai** community.
**Separatist** = state within India (Gorkhaland, Bodoland).

117.s: Which form of communalism uses religion for securing votes?
117.x: Political communalism uses religion for votes; economic communalism grows from competition for jobs and resources.

117.s: Claiming that STs, Jains, Sikhs and Buddhists are Hindus illustrates which dimension of communalism?
117.x: Assimilationist communalism absorbs small religious groups into a larger one.
117.tq: one-liner

117.s: In T.K. Oommen's scheme, what is the communalism that tries to harm members of other communities called?
117.x: Retaliatory communalism tries to harm members of other communities, as in riots and revenge cycles.
117.tq: one-liner

117.s: In T.K. Oommen's classification, the Bahai community keeping away from politics is an example of which dimension of communalism?
117.x: Retreatist communalism is when a small community keeps away from politics, as the Bahai community does.

117.s: In T.K. Oommen's classification, the Gorkhaland demand is an example of which dimension of communalism?
117.x: Separatist communalism seeks a separate territorial state within India, such as Gorkhaland; secessionist seeks one outside India.

117.s: Which of the following distinguishes religious fundamentalism from communalism?
o: Fundamentalism is mainly doctrinal and seeks a return to literal scripture, whereas communalism politically mobilises religious identity against other communities.
Fundamentalism is always directed against another community, whereas communalism reforms one's own community.
Communalism is concerned only with religious doctrine and is unrelated to power or resources.
Fundamentalism and communalism both necessarily involve inter-group conflict.
117.x: Religious fundamentalism is mainly doctrinal, emphasising a return to fundamentals and literal scripture. Communalism is political mobilisation of religious identity against other communities to seek power and resources.
117.tq: Discriminate between look-alike concepts by comparing their direction, objective and method.
xs: **Fundamentalism** is mainly **doctrinal** (return to literal scripture); **communalism** is **political mobilisation of religious identity against other communities** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Fundamentalism is aimed at **reforming one's own community**; communalism at **other communities**, seeking power and resources.
Fundamentalism **can exist without inter-group conflict**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Communalism is **always relational** — "us vs them".
Fundamentalism is often **anti-modern**.
**Political** communalism uses religion for **votes**.

117.s: Which of the following can exist without inter-group conflict?
117.x: Religious fundamentalism can exist without inter-group conflict; communalism is always relational, an 'us versus them' relationship.

117.s: Which of the following is NOT a cause of religious fundamentalism?
117.x: Group exclusiveness is a feature of fundamentalism, not a cause; identity crisis and social insecurity (with globalisation) are causes.
n: Identity crisis is a cause of religious fundamentalism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Religious fundamentalism involves group exclusiveness. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Globalization is a cause of religious fundamentalism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Social insecurity is a cause of religious fundamentalism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]

117.s: Which of the following is a feature of religious fundamentalism?
117.x: Fundamentalism is marked by group exclusiveness, literal reading of scripture, conservatism and resistance to change.
n: Religious fundamentalism involves group exclusiveness. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Religious fundamentalism involves the literal interpretation of scriptures. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Religious fundamentalism involves religious conservatism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Religious fundamentalism involves resistance to change. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]

xs: **Anti-Sikh riots — 1984 — Delhi**, also **Kanpur and Bokaro** — so option **(1)** is correct.

118.x: The 2020 riots took place in North-East Delhi; Muzaffarnagar was 2013, Kokrajhar 2012 and Bhagalpur 1989.

118.s: Which of the following is not true about Justice G. T. Nanavati, who was appointed to enquire into the Godhra train carnage and the Gujarat communal riots?
o: He served as Chief Justice of Karnataka
He served as Chief Justice of Orissa High Court
He served as a member of the Enquiry Commission on the anti-Sikh riots of 1984

118.x: Justice G.T. Nanavati was Chief Justice of Orissa (1994) and Karnataka (1994-95) High Courts, and headed the one-man Nanavati Commission (2000) on the 1984 anti-Sikh riots; he was never Chief Justice of the Madras High Court (printed key: C).

118.s: Which commission was appointed to inquire into the demolition of the disputed structure at Ayodhya on 6 December 1992?
118.x: The Liberhan Commission investigated the demolition of the disputed structure at Ayodhya on 6 December 1992.
118.tq: Directly identify the commission from the matter it was constituted to probe.
xs: The **Liberhan Commission** probed the **demolition of the disputed structure** at Ayodhya on **6 Dec 1992** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jain** = Rajiv Gandhi assassination conspiracy; **Nanavati** = **1984 anti-Sikh riots**; **Srikrishna** = **Bombay riots 1992-93**.
xa: Liberhan was a **one-man commission** set up on **16 Dec 1992**.

118.s: What did the Srikrishna Commission mainly investigate?
118.x: The Srikrishna Commission investigated the Bombay, now Mumbai, riots of 1992–93 and found failure of state administration.
118.tq: Use the commission–riot pair rather than confusing it with other inquiry commissions.
xs: The **Srikrishna Commission** probed the **Bombay riots of 1992-93** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It found **failure of state administration**.
**1984 riots** = **Nanavati**; **Gujarat 2002** = **Nanavati-Mehta**; **Ayodhya demolition** = **Liberhan**.
xa: Liberhan: **one-man** commission, set up **16 Dec 1992**.

118.s: The murder of missionary Graham Staines in Odisha (1999) was inquired into by which commission?
118.x: The Wadhwa Commission probed the murder of Graham Staines (UPSC 2002 PYQ). The Jain Commission probed the conspiracy behind Rajiv Gandhi's assassination. The Srikrishna Commission probed the Bombay riots of 1992-93, and the Liberhan Commission probed the Babri Masjid demolition.
xs: The **Wadhwa Commission** probed the murder of missionary **Graham Staines** (Odisha, **1999**) — so option **(2)** is correct (UPSC **2002** PYQ).
**Jain** = **Rajiv Gandhi** assassination conspiracy; **Srikrishna** = **Bombay riots 1992-93**; **Liberhan** = **Babri demolition**.
xa: **Nanavati** = **1984** anti-Sikh riots; **Nanavati-Mehta** = Gujarat **2002**.
**Ranganath Misra** (NCRLM): religious and linguistic minorities, report **2007**.

118.s: What did the Nanavati Commission (2000) inquire into?
118.x: The Nanavati Commission (2000) probed the 1984 anti-Sikh riots and reported in February 2005; Godhra and Gujarat 2002 went to the Nanavati-Mehta Commission.

118.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Ranganath Misra Commission (1985) — 1984 anti-Sikh riots and Punjab Accord
Ranganath Misra Commission — demolition of the disputed structure at Ayodhya
Wadhwa Commission — conspiracy behind Rajiv Gandhi’s assassination
Jain Commission — murder of Graham Staines
118.x: The Ranganath Misra Commission of 1985 examined the 1984 anti-Sikh riots in the context of the Punjab Accord. The Wadhwa Commission concerned Graham Staines’ murder, while the Jain Commission examined the conspiracy behind Rajiv Gandhi’s assassination.

xs: **Ranganath Misra Commission (1985) — 1984 anti-Sikh riots and Punjab Accord** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.

**Wadhwa** probed **Graham Staines**' murder; **Jain** probed the **Rajiv Gandhi** assassination conspiracy — options (3) and (4) are swapped.

125.x: Under Section 39 of the PHRA, every member and officer of the Commission or a State Commission is deemed a public servant within Sec. 21 IPC.

125.x: Under the PHRA, 'armed forces' means the naval, military and air forces and other armed forces of the Union; armed forces of the State are not included.

125.x: Under Section 31 of the PHRA, the State Government may appoint as Special Public Prosecutor for a Human Rights Court an advocate with not less than seven years' practice.

125.x: Section 2(1)(m) of the PHRA defines 'public servant' (by reference to Sec. 21 IPC), so Section 2(M) is correct. Sec. 2(1)(a) defines armed forces, Sec. 2(1)(h) Member.

125.s: Under which Article of the Constitution the Protection of Human Rights Ordinance was issued by the President in 1993?
125.x: The President promulgated the Protection of Human Rights Ordinance, 1993 under Article 123 (ordinance power) on 28 September 1993. Art. 124 is the Supreme Court, Arts. 125 and 127 judges' salaries and ad hoc judges.

125.x: When an offence under IPC sections 175, 178, 179, 180 or 228 is committed before it, the Commission is deemed a civil court (Sec. 13 PHRA) and may forward the case to a Magistrate.

125.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the mechanisms under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993?
o: The NHRC functions at the State level.
The NHRC functions at the national level.
SHRCs function at the State level.
Human Rights Courts provide a district-level mechanism for speedy trials.
125.x: The NHRC is a national body; State-level work is done by the SHRCs.
n: The NHRC operates at the national level under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The State Human Rights Commission (SHRC) operates at the state level under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
Human Rights Courts provide a district- or trial-level mechanism for speedy trials. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
xa: **Sec. 31**: an advocate of **not less than 7 years** may be a **Special Public Prosecutor**.

125.s: What does the expression 'International Covenants' under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 refer to?

xs: Under **Sec. 2(1)(f)**, "International Covenants" = the **ICCPR and ICESCR** — option **(1)**.
The **UDHR** is a declaration, not a covenant; the **Paris Principles** guide NHRIs.
xa: Both were adopted by the UNGA on **16 Dec 1966**.
**Sec. 2(1)(d)**: human rights = rights to **life, liberty, equality and dignity**.
India is party to the **ICCPR since 1979**.

125.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the dates associated with the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993?

xs: **Ordinance: 28 Sept 1993**; **NHRC constituted: 12 October 1993** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) swaps the two; **20 Dec 1993** is the **UNGA endorsement** of the Paris Principles.
xa: The Act is deemed in force from **28 September 1993**.

125.s: Under the PHRA, 1993, 'human rights' are rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity that are:

125.tq: Armed forces = Union forces only; State armed police excluded.
xs: **State armed police** are **not included** in "armed forces" — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 2(1)(a)**: armed forces = **naval, military and air forces**, including **other armed forces of the Union**.
xa: **Sec. 2(1)(d)** defines human rights — **life, liberty, equality and dignity**.
**Sec. 39**: members and officers deemed **public servants**.
**Sec. 3 / 21**: constitution of **NHRC / SHRC**.

125.s: With whose concurrence does the State Government notify a Court of Session as a Human Rights Court?

xa: **Sec. 31**: **Special Public Prosecutor** — a Public Prosecutor or advocate of **not less than 7 years**.
The Act's objective: **NHRC + SHRCs + Human Rights Courts**.
Commission has **civil court powers under CPC 1908**.

125.s: For offences relating to what are proceedings of a Human Rights Commission deemed judicial proceedings?
o: Bribery and criminal breach of trust
False evidence and insulting a public servant in judicial proceedings
125.x: They are deemed judicial proceedings for false evidence (IPC 193) and insulting a public servant in judicial proceedings (IPC 228); corresponding BNS provisions apply from 1 July 2024.
xa: **Civil court powers under CPC 1908**: summons, documents, affidavits, public records.
**Sec. 39**: members and officers are **public servants** (**Sec. 2(28) BNS**).
**Sec. 30**: **Human Rights Courts** for speedy trial.

125.x: Article 21 has been read to include a decent environment with pollution-free water and air and the right to live with human dignity (Maneka Gandhi). Arts. 20, 22 and 23 deal with conviction, arrest and exploitation.

125.s: The Supreme Court of India has expanded the meaning of the Right to Life to include the following derivative rights. Which one among the following is not included in the court’s definition?
o: Right to Food and Adequate Livelihood
Right to Live in a Healthy Environment

Most books and keys: Right to Health and Information. Strictly: Laxmikanth lists both the right to health and the right to information among rights read into Art. 21, so every option is in the court's definition (Laxmikanth 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01) p.148-149).

125.s:
Which of the following statements are true for the Fundamental Right to Life and Personal Liberty as guaranteed under Article-21 of the Constitution of India?

II. It covers protection against arbitrary executive and legislative action.

III. It includes the right to live with human dignity.

125.x: All four hold: Art. 21 extends to citizens and aliens; after Maneka Gandhi it guards against arbitrary executive and legislative action; it includes life with dignity; and it can be curtailed only by procedure established by law.

125.s: To what do the arrest safeguards laid down in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal primarily relate?

Protection of persons during arrest and custodial detention

**CEDAW** guidelines came from **Vishaka**; manual scavengers are covered by the **2013** Act.
xa: ⚠ **1997** = **Vishaka** and **D.K. Basu**.

**Guruvayur Devaswom (2003)** — courts may rely on international conventions.

125.x: K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy under Article 21; D.K. Basu laid down arrest safeguards.

125.x: In Olga Tellis (1985), the pavement dwellers case, the Supreme Court held that the right to life includes the right to livelihood.

125.x: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) read the right to live with human dignity into Article 21.

125.x: The Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, 42nd Amendment 1976) are in consonance with the UDHR, whose Art. 29 says everyone has duties to the community. CEDAW, WIPO and WTO have no such link.

2. Directive Principles of State Policy
3. Fundamental duties

125.x: The Preamble (justice, liberty, equality, dignity), the DPSPs (work, living wage, education, health) and the Fundamental Duties (UDHR Art. 29: duties to the community) all reflect the UDHR, so 1, 2 and 3.

125.s: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities?
125.x: Article 43 (DPSP) asks the State to secure a living wage, a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities. Art. 42 is humane conditions and maternity relief; Art. 39 livelihood and equal pay; Art. 40 panchayats.

125.s:
Consider the following parts of the Indian Constitution:
1. Preamble
2. Directive Principles of State Policy
3. Fundamental Duties

126.s:
Which of the following statements/statements is/are correct in relation to the Human Rights Commissions in India?

I. The role to undertake functions relating to human rights in the Union Territory of Ladakh may be conferred upon a State Human Rights Commission by the Central Government.

II. Only 2 persons can be appointed as members of the National Human Rights Commission under the category of possessing knowledge or practical experience with respect to human rights.

III. The President can remove the Chairperson of the State Human Rights Commission on the ground of proved misbehaviour. However, the President has to seek the opinion of the Supreme Court in this matter.

IV. The National Human Rights Commission is not empowered to inquire into any matter after the expiry of two years from the date on which the act constituting violation of human rights is alleged to have been committed.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
126.x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (Only III); it is added as option 5.

I is wrong (UT functions cannot go to an SHRC for Delhi, J&K or Ladakh), II is wrong (three human-rights members since 2019), IV is wrong (time bar is one year). (Printed key: None.)

o: the Chief Justice of the High Court of the concerned
the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of India

The Chairperson of the National Human Rights

o: Enquire suo-moto the violation of Human Rights
Review the protection of Human Rights
To punish for the violation of Human Rights

o: issue orders for payment or damages to the complainant/victim
it may recommend to the concerned Government or authority to pay damages

NHRC selection committee — headed by the Chief Minister

SHRC members — appointed by the Governor

o: Strength of the SHRC – Three members including the Chairperson

o: Parliament with a memorandum of action taken
State Legislature with a memorandum of action taken

xs: The NHRC conforms to the **Paris Principles** — option **(2)**.

126.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Paris Principles?
o: They prescribe the procedure for prosecuting custodial deaths before Human Rights Courts.
They prescribe standards of independence, pluralism and a broad mandate for national human-rights institutions.

xa: The **PHRA, 1993** was framed in their light.
**GANHRI** accredits NHRIs as **"A"** (fully compliant) or **"B"**.

126.s: A sitting Judge of the Supreme Court or a sitting Chief Justice of a High Court can be appointed to the NHRC only after consultation with whom?

xa: Term: **3 years or age 70** (since **2019**).

126.s: The Chairperson and members of the NHRC are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Prime Minister. Which one of the following is NOT a member of that committee?

Members are **removed by the President**.

126.s: Which office-holder of the Rajya Sabha is a member of the NHRC selection committee besides its Leader of Opposition?
126.x: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha sits on the six-member PM-led committee; the Chairman (Vice-President) does not.
