The Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Deputy Chairman represents the Rajya Sabha on the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]

126.s: Under the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019, what is the position on reappointment of NHRC members?
o: is limited to the Chairperson for one further term
is barred after the first term
is permitted, the earlier five-year limit having been removed
needs a compulsory gap of five years
126.x: The 2019 amendment removed the earlier five-year limit, so members remain eligible for reappointment, subject to the 3-year/70 term.
xa: Term after 2019: **3 years or 70**.
⚠ "Member is not eligible for re-appointment" is the wrong statement (MPPSC).
After office: **ineligible for further government employment**.

126.s: The NHRC selection committee under Section 4 has how many members?
126.x: The Section 4 committee has six members, headed by the Prime Minister.

126.s: Who appoints the Chairperson and members of the National Human Rights Commission?
126.x: The President appoints them on the advice of a six-member committee headed by the Prime Minister.

126.s:
Consider the following statements about the removal of the NHRC Chairperson:
1. The President can remove the Chairperson directly if he is adjudged an insolvent.
2. Removal for proved misbehaviour or incapacity needs an inquiry by the Supreme Court on the President's reference.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
126.x: Insolvency, paid outside employment, infirmity, unsound mind and moral-turpitude conviction allow direct removal; misbehaviour or incapacity needs a Supreme Court inquiry.

126.s: Which of the following is NOT a ground on which the President may remove the Chairperson of the NHRC?
o: Engaging in paid employment outside the duties of office
Conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude
Being of unsound mind as declared by a competent court
Disagreeing with the policies of the Union Government
126.x: The Act lists insolvency, paid outside employment, infirmity, unsound mind, moral-turpitude conviction, and proved misbehaviour or incapacity; policy disagreement is not a ground.

126.s: As part of its work related to protection of human rights, on which disease, did the National Human Rights Commission take various initiatives including submission of a special report to the Parliament?
126.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-II Screening Test 2017
126.x: The NHRC took up silicosis (a lung disease of mine and quarry workers) and submitted a special report on it to Parliament. Dengue, heat stroke and leprosy were not the subject of such a report.

126.s: Analyze the statements with reference to National Human Rights Commission : (i) The Human Rights Commission, encourages organizations working in the field of Human Rights. (ii) The work of the Commission is also to conduct research in the field of Human Rights. Answer from the following.
o: Statement (i) is the correct explanation of Statement
126.x: Section 12 functions include encouraging NGOs working in human rights and undertaking and promoting research, so both statements are true (neither explains the other).

126.s: Which of the following is NOT a function of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) as per the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993?
o: Inquiring into complaints of human rights violations, either suo motu or on a petition by a victim or any person on their behalf.
Intervening in any court proceeding involving allegations of human rights violations, without the court's approval.
Visiting jails and other institutions under Central Government only, and studying the living conditions of inmates and making recommendations.
Undertaking and promoting research in the field of human rights.
126.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer (A.P. Tribal Welfare
126.x:
Printed key: option 2 (intervene without court approval). Strictly: the jail-visit option is also inaccurate, because the power covers jails under the State Government too, not 'Central Government only' (PHRA s.12(c); general knowledge, not checked).
The NHRC can intervene in court proceedings only with the court's approval, so 'without the court's approval' is not a function. Inquiries (suo motu or on petition) and research are functions.

126.s: During an inquiry, for which purpose does a Human Rights Commission have the powers of a civil court under the CPC, 1908?
o: Reviewing judgments of the High Courts
Awarding imprisonment to guilty public servants
126.x: The Commission has civil-court powers such as summons, requiring documents, receiving affidavits and requisitioning public records; it has no sentencing powers.
xa: Proceedings are deemed **judicial** for false evidence (**s.193**) and insulting a public servant (**s.228**).
Since **1 July 2024** these read as the corresponding **BNS/BNSS** provisions.
**NHRC advice is non-binding** — a common criticism.

126.s: The Supreme Court entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the implementation of which law in 1997?
o: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
126.x: In 1997, the Supreme Court entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
126.tq: Pair the judicial direction with the exact statute rather than a neighbouring social-justice law.
xs: In **1997** the SC entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the **Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976** — option **(3)**.
It is one of the NHRC's **specialised mandates**, alongside custodial and encounter deaths.
xa: **Custodial deaths**: report within **24 hours**; post-mortem videography.
**Encounter deaths**: reporting + magisterial inquiry per **PUCL v Maharashtra (2014)**.
**Transgender welfare**: **Advisory 2.0** (May **2026**).

126.s: With whose approval can the NHRC intervene in court proceedings involving human-rights allegations?
126.x: It needs the approval of the court concerned, not the Central Government.
xa: Since 2006 it may also recommend **interim relief even during inquiry**.
2006 also enabled the NHRC to **transfer complaints** to the concerned SHRC.
Custodial deaths must be reported within **24 hours**.

126.s: Which of the following is a power of the NHRC?
o: Visiting jails to study inmates' living conditions
Unrestricted investigation of the armed forces
126.x: The NHRC may visit jails and has civil-court powers, but its recommendations are advisory and it cannot directly investigate the armed forces.
n: The NHRC has all the powers of a civil court while inquiring into complaints. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC visits jails and detention centres to study the living conditions of inmates. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The recommendations of the NHRC are advisory in nature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The recommendations of the NHRC are recommendatory in nature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC does not directly execute criminal sentencing. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC does not have direct or unrestricted investigative powers over the armed forces. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC suggests reforms based on its study of jail and detention-centre conditions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC does not act as a regular court of law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
xa: **Time bar**: no inquiry **after one year** from the alleged act.
⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces).
Since **2006**, NHRC may visit jails **even without intimating the State Govt**.

126.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about how the NHRC may take up an inquiry?
o: It may take suo motu cognisance.
It may inquire into a complaint solely against a private individual with no public servant involved.
It may act on a petition presented to it.
It may act on a direction of a court.
126.x: The NHRC's jurisdiction concerns violations or negligence by public servants, so a purely private complaint is outside it.
xa: It may **intervene** in court proceedings with the **court's approval**.
Time bar: no inquiry **after one year** from the alleged act.
Sub judice matters are not taken up.

126.s: While inquiring into complaints, the NHRC has the powers of which court?
126.x: The NHRC has civil-court powers such as summoning persons, examining them on oath, requiring documents and requisitioning public records.
xa: It can also **receive evidence on affidavit**.
The **SHRC** has the same inquiry powers.
Yet it has **no power to punish** violators.

126.s: Which of the following can the National Human Rights Commission do with respect to relief?
o: Grant relief only after a criminal court records conviction
Recommend compensation and interim relief, including during the inquiry
Punish the public servant and recover the amount directly
Award final compensation in every case without recommendation
126.x: The NHRC may recommend compensation, prosecution and interim relief. Since the 2006 amendment, it may recommend interim relief even during the inquiry.
126.tq: Apply the distinction between recommending relief and directly awarding or enforcing it.
xs: The NHRC may **recommend compensation and interim relief**, including **during the inquiry** — option **(2)** (since **2006**).
It cannot itself **punish** or award final compensation; it only recommends.
xa: It may also recommend **prosecution**.
Government must inform it of **action taken within one month**.
Armed forces: Centre informs it of action within **three months**.

126.s: What is the nature of the recommendations of the NHRC?
o: Binding decrees of a civil court
A source of automatic criminal liability
Advisory, though the Government must inform it of action taken
126.x: NHRC recommendations are advisory and cannot be compelled; the Government must only inform the Commission of the action taken.

126.s: Since 2006, on what condition may the NHRC visit jails and detention centres?
126.x: The 2006 amendment let the NHRC visit jails without intimating the State Government.

126.s: In which case did the Supreme Court lay down 16-point guidelines on encounter deaths in 2014?
o: D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal
Prakash Singh v Union of India
Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa
126.x: PUCL v State of Maharashtra (2014) set 16-point guidelines on encounter deaths, used with NHRC reporting norms.

126.s: The NHRC's Advisory 2.0 issued in May 2026 concerns the welfare of which group?
126.x: Advisory 2.0 (May 2026) is on transgender welfare: Census categories, legal-aid cells and Garima Greh expansion.

126.s: Which of the following is a function of the NHRC under Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act?
o: Reviewing factors, including acts of terrorism, that inhibit the enjoyment of human rights
Punishing public servants found guilty of violations
Appointing the Chairpersons of State Human Rights Commissions
Framing laws on human rights for Parliament
126.x: Section 12 lets the NHRC review safeguards and factors such as terrorism that inhibit human rights; it cannot punish or legislate.

126.s: After the NHRC sends its inquiry report with recommendations, within what period must the Government concerned inform the Commission of the action taken?
126.x: The Government must inform the Commission of the action taken on its report within one month. Three months is the period for the Central Government to report action in armed-forces cases; six months and one year are not the prescribed periods (one year is the time bar for inquiry).
xs: The Government must inform the NHRC of **action taken within one month** — option **(1)**.
**Three months** applies to the Centre in **armed-forces** cases; **one year** is the **time bar** for inquiries.
xa: ⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces); time bar **one year**.
Recommendations are **advisory**.
NHRC annual report is laid before **each House of Parliament** with a memorandum of action taken.

126.s:
With reference to the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019, consider the following statements about National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) :

I. Judge of the Supreme Court can now be appointed as Chairperson of the Commission.

II. Term of the Chairperson and members shall be three years.

III. Chairperson and members shall be eligible for re-appointment.
126.x: The 2019 amendment made a former SC Judge eligible as Chairperson, cut the term to three years and allowed reappointment, so I, II and III.

126.s: In every District ______ may be specified as a Human rights court
126.x: Under Section 30 of the PHRA, the State Government, with the HC Chief Justice's concurrence, specifies a Court of Session in each district as a Human Rights Court. Collectorates, panchayats and gram sabhas are not courts.

126.s: Under which Section of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 are Human Rights Courts provided for?
126.x: Section 30 deals with Human Rights Courts; Section 31 covers Special Public Prosecutors, Section 3 the NHRC and Section 21 the SHRC.
xa: Public servant: **Sec. 21 IPC** → now **Sec. 2(28) BNS** (from **1 July 2024**).
Sec. 31: advocate in practice for **not less than 7 years**.

126.s: To how many years did the 2019 amendment reduce the term of the NHRC Chairperson and members from 5 years?
126.x: The term was cut from 5 to 3 years (or age 70), and reappointment is allowed.

126.s:
Consider the following statements about the 2019 amendment to the PHRA:
1. Human-rights members of the NHRC rose from 2 to 3, one being a woman.
2. Any High Court judge can now chair an SHRC.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
126.x: Both are correct: members rose from 2 to 3 including a woman, and an SHRC chair can now be any HC judge as well.

126.s: What did the 2006 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act enable the NHRC to do?
o: Convert every district court into a Human Rights Court
Transfer all NHRC members to State service
Transfer complaints to the concerned SHRC
126.x: The 2006 amendment enabled the NHRC to transfer complaints to the concerned State Human Rights Commission.
126.tq: Identify the precise transfer power and reject broader institutional powers not stated in the law.
xs: The **2006 amendment** enabled the NHRC to **transfer complaints** to the concerned **SHRC** — option **(4)**.
It gave no power to dissolve SHRCs or move members; **Human Rights Courts** are notified by the State Govt under the PHRA.
xa: Other 2006 changes: **NCSC and NCST** chairs as deemed members; jail visits **without intimating the State Govt**.
Also: **interim relief** even **during inquiry**; SHRC cut from **five to three**.
Resignation: NHRC → **President**, SHRC → **Governor**.

126.s: With whose concurrence does the State Government notify Human Rights Courts under Section 30?
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
126.x: The State Government, with the HC Chief Justice's concurrence, notifies a Court of Session in each district as a Human Rights Court.

126.s: For at least how many years must a Special Public Prosecutor for a Human Rights Court (Section 31) have practised as an advocate?
126.x: Section 31 requires an advocate of seven years' practice.

126.s: Which of the following was NOT a change made by the 2006 amendment?
o: Jail visits without intimating the State Government
Reducing the term of NHRC members to three years
Transfer of complaints to the SHRC concerned
126.x: The term was cut from five to three years (or 70) by the 2019 amendment, not in 2006.

126.s: Before which body is the annual report of the NHRC laid, with a memorandum of action taken?
126.x: The NHRC report goes to the Central Government and is laid before each House of Parliament.

126.s: Under GANHRI accreditation, what does 'A' status mean for a national human rights institution?
o: Partly compliant with the Paris Principles
Fully compliant with the Paris Principles
126.x: GANHRI's Sub-Committee on Accreditation gives 'A' for full and 'B' for partial compliance with the Paris Principles.

126.s:
Consider the following statements about NHRC-India and GANHRI:
1. In May 2024 GANHRI deferred NHRC-India's re-accreditation for the second year in a row.
2. The deferral cited the NHRC's independence from government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
126.x: Both are correct: GANHRI deferred re-accreditation in 2023 and again in May 2024, citing independence from government; the NHRC says its 'A' status continues.

126.s: While dealing with complaints of violation of Human Rights by the members of the armed forces, the Commission either on its own motion or on receipt of a petition will?
o: give directions to the concerned police officers to
seek a report from the Central Government
126.x: For complaints against members of the armed forces, the Commission seeks a report from the Central Government and makes recommendations; it cannot probe them itself.

126.s: What is the nature of the advice of the National Human Rights Commission to the Government?
o: Binding on both Union and States
126.x: NHRC advice is non-binding on the Government; the NHRC is a statutory body.

126.s: Under the statutory procedure concerning the armed forces, what does the NHRC do?
o: It calls for an independent report from the Central Government and makes recommendations based on that report
It transfers every complaint to the SHRC for investigation
It directly imposes criminal sentencing on members of the armed forces
It directly investigates all complaints without restriction
126.x: For the armed forces, the NHRC cannot investigate directly. It asks the Central Government for a report and makes recommendations on it.
126.tq: Recall the NHRC's limited role over the armed forces.
n: The NHRC does not directly execute criminal sentencing. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC does not have direct or unrestricted investigative powers over the armed forces. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
Under the statutory procedure, the NHRC calls for an independent report from the Central Government regarding the armed forces. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC makes recommendations based on the report from the Central Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
xs: For the **armed forces**, the NHRC **calls for an independent report from the Central Government** and **makes recommendations** — option **(1)**.
It has **no direct or unrestricted investigative** powers over them.
It does **not** execute **criminal sentencing**; its recommendations are **advisory**.
xa: **Armed forces** = **naval**, **military** and **air** forces and other Union armed forces.
⚠ Sources differ on the section: **Section 2(m)** vs **Sec. 2(1)(a)**.
**State armed police** are **not included** in "armed forces".

126.s: The NHRC cannot inquire into a matter after how long from the date of the alleged act?
126.x: The NHRC is barred after one year from the alleged act; a review committee wanted this relaxed where sufficient cause exists.
xa: The **SHRC** is subject to the same **one-year bar**.
⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces).
The time bar is part of the "**toothless tiger**" criticism.

126.s: Why is the NHRC criticised as a 'toothless tiger'?
o: It lacks civil-court powers during inquiries
It is not a statutory body
126.x: The criticism rests on its non-binding advice, along with the one-year bar and limits on armed-forces complaints.
xa: The NHRC has **no power to punish** violators.
**Allahabad HC** said the NHRC exceeded its mandate by directing an EOW probe into **558** aided madrasas (**30 Apr 2026**).
SHRCs are weakened by **optional creation**, **advisory powers** and **vacancies**.

126.s: In cases concerning the armed forces, within what period must the Central Government inform the NHRC of the action taken?
126.x: In armed-forces cases, the Central Government must inform the NHRC of the action taken within three months.
126.tq: Distinguish the armed-forces response period from the general one-month reporting period.
xs: In **armed-forces** cases the Centre must inform the NHRC of action taken within **three months** — option **(2)**.
**One month** is the general action-taken period; **one year** is the time bar for inquiries.
xa: ⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces); time bar **one year**.
In armed-forces cases the NHRC may only **seek a report from the Central Government** and recommend.
"Armed forces" = **naval, military and air forces**, incl. other armed forces of the Union (**Sec. 2**).

127.s: In 2016, in the case of Youth Bar Association of India (Yuva Nyavaadula Sangham), the Supreme Court delivered a judgement that except in certain sensitive matters, in all cases copies of FIRs shall be
o: Handed over to the person and relatives within 24 hours of registration
Uploaded to the police website/State website within 24 hours of registration
Filed in the Court within 24 hours of registration
Should not be revealed without the permission of the Court
127.src: APPSC Asst. Social, BC & Tribal Welfare Officers Screening T
127.x: In Youth Bar Association of India v Union of India (2016) the SC directed that FIR copies, except in sensitive cases, be uploaded on the police or State website within 24 hours of registration.

127.s:
With reference to India, consider the following statements:

1. Judicial custody means an accused is in the custody of the concerned magistrate and such accused is locked up in police station, not in jail.

2. During judicial custody, the police officer in charge of the case is not allowed to interrogate the suspect without the approval of the court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
127.x: Statement 1 is wrong: in judicial custody the accused is lodged in jail under the magistrate's custody, not in the police station. Statement 2 is right: police cannot interrogate the accused without the court's approval.

127.s:
With reference to India, consider the following statements:

1. When a prisoner makes out a sufficient case, parole cannot be denied to such prisoner because it becomes a matter of his/her right.

2. State Governments have their own Prisoners Release on Parole Rules.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
127.x: Parole is not a matter of right even when a case is made out; it is a concession. State Governments have their own Prisoners Release on Parole Rules, so 2 only.

127.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Statement-I: In India, prisons are managed by State Governments with their own rules and regulations for the day-to-day administration of prisons.
2. Statement-II: In India, prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 which expressly kept the subject of prisons in the control of Provincial Governments. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is the correct
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
127.x: Prisons are a State subject (State List Entry 4), so States run them with their own rules; the Prisons Act 1894 placed prisons under the Provincial (now State) Governments, which explains Statement I.

127.s: Consider the following statements : Statement-I : In India, prisons are managed by State Governments with their own rules and regulations for the dayto-day administration of prisons. Statement-II : In India, prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 which expressly kept the subject of prisons in the control of Provincial Governments. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct

127.s: Under the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, prisons are included in which of the following?
127.x: Prisons are a State subject under Entry 4 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule.
127.tq: Test the exact List and Entry instead of relying on the general subject classification.
xs: **Prisons** are in the **State List, Entry 4** of the Seventh Schedule — option **(4)**.
They are not a Union or Concurrent subject.
xa: Prisons are governed by the **Prisons Act 1894** and **State jail manuals**.
**BPR&D** issues **advisory** guidelines.
**Model Prisons Act 2023** — prepared by **MHA** as a guide for States.

127.s: The Model Prisons Act, 2023 guides States in replacing the colonial Prisons Act of which year?
127.x: The MHA's Model Prisons Act, 2023 is meant to replace the Prisons Act, 1894; it is not automatically binding on States.
xa: Prisons = **State List, Entry 4**.
**BPR&D** issues advisory guidelines.
Justice **Amitava Roy Committee** (**2018**): overcrowding, undertrials, legal aid, speedy trial.

127.s: Under BNSS Section 479, an undertrial is generally eligible for release after serving what part of the maximum term?
127.x: BNSS Section 479 provides release after one-half of the maximum term, reduced to one-third for first-time offenders, subject to statutory conditions.
xa: Undertrials are **~73%** of inmates; **9,028** held over **5 years** (NCRB **2024**).
The **Justice Amitava Roy Committee** (**2018**) addressed undertrials and speedy trial.
The **Mulla Committee** wanted **separate undertrials**.

127.s: Which body issues advisory guidelines on prison administration, alongside the Prisons Act, 1894 and State jail manuals?
127.x: Prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 and State jail manuals, while BPR&D issues advisory guidelines.

127.s: According to NCRB Prison Statistics 2024, what were the prison occupancy rate and the proportion of undertrials respectively?
127.x: NCRB Prison Statistics 2024 reported prison occupancy at 112.7%, with undertrials constituting 73% of the prison population.
127.tq: Keep the percentage pair together and reject options that alter one figure while retaining the other.
xs: NCRB **2024**: occupancy **112.7%** and undertrials **73%** — option **(4)**.
**112.7%** is a **decade-low**; the other percentages are not in the data.
xa: **Delhi** highest occupancy **194.6%**, **Meghalaya** **163.5%**.
**9,028** undertrials held over **5 years**.
Released on **3 Jun 2026**.

127.s: With reference to parole and furlough, which one of the following is correct?
o: They are available only to undertrial prisoners.
They are governed by identical Central rules applicable to every State.
They are not absolute rights, and each State has its own prisoner-release rules.
They constitute an absolute constitutional right available uniformly throughout India.
127.x: Parole and furlough are not absolute rights. Each State frames its own prisoner-release or parole rules.

xs: Parole and furlough are **not absolute rights**, and **each State has its own prisoner-release rules** — option **(3)** (UPSC **2021**: the only correct statement).

xa: Prisons are a **State List (Entry 4)** subject.
**BNSS s.479**: undertrial release after **half** the maximum term (**one-third** for first-time offenders).
SC (**Aug 2025**): immediate release of prisoners held beyond sentence completion.

127.s: What is the status of the Model Prisons Act, 2023, prepared by the MHA?
o: A guide not binding on States
A Central law replacing State jail manuals
127.x: The Model Prisons Act, 2023 is an MHA guide for replacing the 1894 Act and is not binding, since prisons are a State subject.

127.s: According to NCRB Prison Statistics 2024, women made up what share of prison inmates?
127.x: Women were 4.14% of inmates, and there are only 34 women's prisons.

127.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about prisons in India?
o: Prisons fall under Entry 4 of the State List
First-time undertrials may be freed after one-third of the maximum term under BNSS s.479
The Prisons Act, 1894 is a colonial law
Parole and furlough are absolute rights of prisoners
127.x: Parole and furlough are not absolute rights; each State has its own rules.

127.s: According to NCRB Prison Statistics 2024, undertrials constituted approximately what share of inmates?
127.x: Undertrials were about 73% of inmates; women were 4.14% and there were only 34 women's prisons.

127.x: Delhi's prisons were the most overcrowded at 194.6% occupancy, ahead of Meghalaya (163.5%); the national rate was 112.7%.

127.s: According to NCRB Prison Statistics 2024, how many prisons were there in India?
127.x: NCRB Prison Statistics 2024: 1,333 prisons, capacity about 4.53 lakh and 5.11 lakh inmates.

127.s: According to NCRB Prison Statistics 2024, how many exclusive women's prisons does India have?
127.x: Women are 4.14% of inmates and India has only 34 women's prisons (NCRB Prison Statistics 2024).

127.s: In which of the following judgements of the Constitutional Bench of the Supreme Court of India, the ‘rarest of rare’ principle in the award of death penalty was first laid down.
o: Bachan Singh Vs State of Punjab (1980)
Dr. Upendra Baxi Vs State of UP (1983)
127.x: The Constitution Bench laid down the 'rarest of rare' doctrine, with life imprisonment as the rule, in Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980); Machhi Singh (1983) later elaborated it.

127.s: In Shatrughan Chauhan v Union of India (2014), what was inordinate, unexplained delay in deciding a mercy petition held to do?
o: Justify commuting death to life imprisonment
127.x: The Court held that unexplained delay in deciding mercy petitions may justify commuting the death sentence to life imprisonment.

127.s: The decision in Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh (2006) is associated with which proposition?
o: Mercy powers are completely immune from judicial scrutiny.
Pardon and remission are open to limited judicial review.
Only the Supreme Court may decide mercy petitions.
A Governor may pardon every death sentence.

128.s: In which year was the Indian Succession Act enacted?

**Vineeta Sharma** (**2020**): daughters are coparceners **by birth**, whether or not the father was alive on **9 Sept 2005**.

128.s: Which Act bans prenatal sex determination to stop female feticide?
128.x: The PCPNDT Act bans sex determination; the MTP Act allows abortion up to 24 weeks on set grounds.

The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act prohibits prenatal sex determination. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #48 · pp 99-101]

Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma clarified the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 96-98]
Daughters have coparcenary rights by birth under the principle clarified in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 96-98]
Shayara Bano v. Union of India declared instant Talaq-e-Biddat unconstitutional. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 96-98]
Shayara Bano v. Union of India held instant Talaq-e-Biddat violative of Article 14. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 96-98]

o: Consent is relevant only if the trafficking is inter-State.

**Palermo Protocol (2000)** supplements **UNTOC**.

130.s: Which provision of the Constitution of India prohibits traffic in human beings?
130.x: Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour. Article 21A is the right to education, Article 24 bars child labour in hazardous employment, and Article 39(f) is a Directive Principle on protecting children from exploitation.

**Palermo Protocol (2000)** supplements **UNTOC**, ratified by India.

o: Article 24 – Prohibits traffic in human beings
Palermo Protocol – Supplements the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime
BNS Section 143 – Victim's consent is necessary
2021 draft trafficking Bill – CBI as national investigating agency

130.s: Under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, which of the following is correct?
o: Prostitution itself is treated as a crime in every circumstance.

xs: ITPA punishes **brothel-keeping, pimping, soliciting** and **living on earnings** — option **(3)**.
Prostitution is **not a crime per se**; protective homes are run **by States**.
xa: It is a **1956** law.
**BNS s.143** defines trafficking.

130.x: The 2021 draft Bill named the NIA as the national investigating agency.

the two-finger test in rape cases

xs: **Andhra Pradesh** was first to sub-categorise SCs **by law** (**AP Act 2000**) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Punjab** did so earlier (**1975**) only **by circular**.
**Telangana** was first to **implement** sub-categorisation after **Davinder Singh** (**April 2025**).
xa: The Act followed the **Justice Ramachandra Raju Commission** (**1996**).
It was struck down in **E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)**.
⚠ **A – B – C – D** = **Relli – Madiga – Mala – Adi-Andhra**.

133.s: Which State became the first to implement Scheduled Caste sub-categorisation after the Davinder Singh judgment?
133.x: Telangana became the first State to implement Scheduled Caste sub-categorisation after Davinder Singh, with three groups in April 2025.
133.tq: Distinguish the State that enacted the earlier framework from the State that implemented the post-2024 classification.
xs: **Telangana** was first to implement SC sub-categorisation after **Davinder Singh** — option **(1)** is correct.
It made **3** groups in **April 2025**.
**AP** was first by law (**2000**), and **Punjab** first by circular (**1975**) — both before the judgment.
xa: **Davinder Singh (2024)** was decided **6:1**.
AP's **Ramachandra Raju Commission (1996)** made **four** groups.

133.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Rajiv Gauba Committee?
o: It concerned SC sub-castes such as the Madigas.
It was a Cabinet Secretary panel constituted in 2024.
It examined equitable mechanisms for the most backward SC sub-castes.
It was set up by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to examine ST status for the Madigas.
133.x: The Gauba panel was a 2024 Cabinet Secretary panel on the most backward SC sub-castes such as the Madigas; it was not a Tribal Affairs body and did not examine ST status.
n: The Rajiv Gauba Committee explored equitable administrative mechanisms for the most backward sub-castes among Scheduled Castes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee was a Cabinet Secretary panel formed in 2024. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee explored alternative interventions for the most backward sub-castes among Scheduled Castes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
Madigas were cited as an example of the most backward Scheduled Caste sub-castes considered by the Rajiv Gauba Committee. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee was formed by the Central Government through the Department of Personnel and Training. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee concerned Scheduled Castes (SCs). [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
xa: **Idate Commission** (**2017**) → **SEED Scheme**.
**K.G. Balakrishnan Commission** extended till **10 June 2026**.
**Davinder Singh** (**2024**) allowed sub-classification within SCs.

133.s: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India states that there shall be a Commission for the Scheduled Tribes to be known as the National Commission for the Scheduled Tribes?
133.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
133.x: Article 338A (89th Amendment, 2003) provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes; 338 is the NCSC.

133.s: The AP State Commission for SCs and STs was established in 2016 by reconstituting the AP State Commission for SCs & STs amending the Act. 9 of _____.
133.x: The AP State Commission for SCs and STs was set up in 2016 by amending Act 9 of 2003.

133.s: "There shall be a National Commission for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to be appointed by the President." Which Article of the Indian Constitution stipulates the above?
133.x: Article 338 (as amended in 1990) provided for a National Commission for SCs and STs appointed by the President; the 89th Amendment (2003) split it into 338 (NCSC) and 338A (NCST).

133.s: What does Article 338(9) of the Constitution provide?
o: It empowers the President to create State Commissions for Scheduled Castes
It requires the Union and every State to consult the National Commission for Scheduled Castes on all major policy matters affecting SCs
It gives the NCSC power to amend the Scheduled Caste list
It provides grants-in-aid to State SC Commissions
133.x: Article 338(9) obliges the Union and State Governments to consult the NCSC on major policy matters affecting SCs. It does not empower the President to create State commissions (a trap in CDCA); State SC Commissions are created by State law. The SC list is altered only by Parliament under Article 341, and grants-in-aid are under Article 275(1) for ST welfare.
133.tq: 338(9) = duty to consult NCSC; State SC Commissions come from State law.
xs: **Art. 338(9)** requires the **Union and every State to consult the NCSC** on major policy matters — option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ CDCA says 338(9) lets the President create State commissions — **wrong**; State SC Commissions are made by **State law**.
The SC list is altered only by **Parliament** (**Art. 341**); grants-in-aid are **Art. 275(1)**.
xa: NCSC and NCST have **civil-court powers** while inquiring.
AP has a statutory **State SC Commission** (chairman **K.S. Jawahar**).

133.s: Under which Article did the 89th Amendment (2003) create the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes?
133.x: The 89th Amendment split the joint commission into the NCSC (Article 338) and NCST (Article 338A); the Commissions report to the President.
xa: Functions: investigate safeguards, inquire into complaints, **advise on planning**.
Powers: **civil-court powers** while inquiring.
Original Art. 338 had a **Special Officer**.

133.s: What did the original form of Article 338 provide for?
o: a non-statutory multi-member commission appointed by the State Governments
a Special Officer designated as the Commissioner for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
a Parliamentary committee for monitoring reservations
a separate National Commission for Scheduled Castes and a separate National Commission for Scheduled Tribes
133.x: Originally, Article 338 provided for a Special Officer, known as the Commissioner for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, to investigate safeguards and report to the President.
133.tq: Track institutional evolution by identifying the original arrangement before later commissions were created.
xs: Original **Art. 338** provided a **Special Officer** (Commissioner for SCs and STs) — option **(2)** is correct.
He **investigated safeguards** and **reported to the President**.
Separate NCSC and NCST came only with the **89th Amendment (2003)**.
xa: **1978 Resolution**: non-statutory multi-member Commission for SCs and STs; modified in **1987**.
**1990**: the joint commission became **constitutional** (**Art. 338**).
**NCST** from **19 Feb 2004**.

133.s: The Chairperson of the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes holds which rank?
133.x: The NCST Chairperson has Cabinet rank, the Vice-Chairperson Minister of State rank, and members Secretary rank.

133.s: Besides the Chairperson and Vice-Chairperson, how many members does the National Commission for Scheduled Castes have?
133.x: Each Commission has a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and 3 members; the President fixes their tenure.
133.tq: one-liner

133.s: From which date did the separate National Commission for Scheduled Tribes come into being?
133.x: After the 89th Amendment (2003) split the joint commission, the NCST came into being on 19 February 2004.
133.tq: one-liner

133.s: In which year did the joint commission for SCs and STs become a constitutional body?
133.x: A non-statutory Commission came in 1978; it became a constitutional joint commission in 1990 and was split in 2003.
133.tq: one-liner

133.s: In which year was the Andhra Pradesh State Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes set up by amending Act 9 of 2003?
133.x: The AP State Commission for SCs and STs was set up in 2016 by amending Act 9 of 2003.

133.s: Who is the chairman of the Andhra Pradesh State Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
133.x: K.S. Jawahar heads the AP State Commission for SCs and STs.

133.s: To whom does the National Commission for Scheduled Castes present its reports?
133.x: The NCSC has civil-court powers and reports to the President.

133.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Statement-I: The Supreme Court of India has held in some judgements that the reservation policies made under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India would be limited by Article 335 for maintenance of efficiency of administration.
2. Statement-II: Article 335 of the Constitution of India defines the term 'efficiency of administration'. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is the correct
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is not the correct
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
133.x: Statement I is correct: the SC has read Art. 16(4) with Art. 335 (efficiency of administration) – Indra Sawhney, M. Nagaraj. Statement II is wrong: Art. 335 uses but does not define 'efficiency of administration'.

133.s: Consider the following statements : Statement-I : The Supreme Court of India has held in some judgements that the reservation policies made under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India would be limited by Article 335 for maintenance of efficiency of administration. Statement-II : Article 335 of the Constitution of India defines the term ‘efficiency of administration’. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
133.x: Statement I is correct: the SC has read Art. 16(4) with Art. 335 (efficiency of administration) – Indra Sawhney, M. Nagaraj. Statement II is wrong: Art. 335 uses but does not define 'efficiency of administration'.

133.s: Which Amendment introduced Article 16(4B), on carrying forward unfilled reserved vacancies as a separate class?
133.x: The 81st Amendment inserted Article 16(4B); such vacancies are not counted against that year's 50% ceiling.
xa: **M. Nagaraj (2006)** upheld the **77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th** Amendments but required **quantifiable data**.
⚠ **77th – 82nd – 85th** = promotion quota – relaxed marks – consequential seniority.

133.s: Article 16(4A), permitting reservation in promotion for SCs and STs, was inserted by the 77th Amendment (1995) mainly in response to which judicial position?
o: Indra Sawhney (1992) confining reservation under Article 16(4) to initial appointment
E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) treating SCs as a homogeneous class
133.x: Indra Sawhney (1992) held that reservation under Article 16(4) applies only at initial appointment, not promotion; the 77th Amendment (1995) responded by inserting Article 16(4A). M. Nagaraj came later and upheld the 77th; Chinnaiah concerns SC sub-classification; Janhit Abhiyan concerns EWS.
133.tq: 77th = 16(4A) promotion, answer to Indra Sawhney.
xs: The **77th Amendment (1995)** responded to **Indra Sawhney (1992)**, which confined **Art. 16(4)** to **initial appointment** — option **(1)** is correct.
**M. Nagaraj (2006)** came later and upheld the 77th; **E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)** concerns SC sub-classification.
xa: Indra Sawhney also set the **50% ceiling**.
**85th** added consequential seniority w.e.f. **17 June 1995**.
**Davinder Singh (2024)** overruled **Chinnaiah**.

133.s: The proviso to Article 335 relating to relaxation of qualifying marks in promotion was enabled by which Constitutional Amendment?
133.x: The Eighty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000 inserted the proviso to Article 335 permitting relaxation of qualifying marks and standards in promotion for SCs and STs.
133.tq: Separate the closely placed reservation amendments by their precise subject.
xs: The **82nd Amendment (2000)** added the proviso to **Art. 335** allowing **relaxed qualifying marks** in promotion — option **(3) Eighty-Second** is correct.
**77th (1995)** = 16(4A) promotion quota; **81st** = 16(4B) carry-forward; **85th** = consequential seniority.
⚠ G2 **2024** circulated key said **89th** — that is the **NCSC-NCST bifurcation** amendment.
xa: **M. Nagaraj (2006)** upheld the 77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th but required **quantifiable data**.
⚠ **77th – 82nd – 85th** = promotion quota – relaxed marks – consequential seniority.

133.s: With which of the following is the 85th Constitutional Amendment associated?
o: relaxation in qualifying marks under Article 335
backlog vacancies being treated as a separate class
consequential seniority in promotion under Article 16(4A), with effect from 17 June 1995
reservation of seats for STs in the Lok Sabha
133.x: The 85th Amendment provided consequential seniority in promotion under Article 16(4A), with effect from 17 June 1995.
133.tq: Use the effective date and the phrase “consequential seniority” as the decisive identifiers.
xs: The **85th Amendment** gave **consequential seniority** in promotion under **16(4A)**, w.e.f. **17 June 1995** — option **(3)** is correct.
Relaxed marks = **82nd**; backlog as a separate class = **81st** (16(4B)); ST Lok Sabha seats = **51st**.
xa: The 85th is dated **2001** (IYB lists **2002**).
**16(4A)** itself was inserted by the **77th (1995)**.
**M. Nagaraj (2006)** upheld the 85th with the **quantifiable data** condition.

133.s: Which case struck down the AP Scheduled Caste (Rationalisation of Reservations) Act, 2000?
o: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
133.x: E.V. Chinnaiah treated SCs as a single class and held that sub-classification interfered with the Article 341 list.

133.s: By what majority did the seven-judge Bench in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) permit sub-classification within Scheduled Castes?
133.x: The Bench permitted sub-classification by 6:1, overruling E.V. Chinnaiah.

133.s: Which case upheld the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Constitutional Amendments, subject to the State showing quantifiable data on specified conditions?
o: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh
133.x: M. Nagaraj upheld the four constitutional amendments but required quantifiable data concerning backwardness, inadequate representation and administrative efficiency.
133.tq: Associate a cluster of constitutional amendments with the case that examined them.
xs: **M. Nagaraj (2006)** upheld the **77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th** Amendments — option **(3)** is correct.
But the State must show **quantifiable data** on **backwardness**, **inadequate representation** and **administrative efficiency**.
**Davinder Singh** and **Chinnaiah** concern **SC sub-classification**.
xa: ⚠ **77th – 82nd – 85th** = promotion quota – relaxed marks – consequential seniority.
**81st** = **16(4B)** carry-forward vacancies.
**Indra Sawhney (1992)** set the **50% ceiling**.

133.s: In August 2026, what was the Centre's position on an income-based creamy layer in SC/ST reservations?
o: It left the decision to State SC Commissions
It said creamy-layer rules already apply to all SC/ST quotas
It opposed it, saying any change needs a holistic empirical review
133.x: The Centre's affidavit opposed an income-based creamy layer in SC/ST quotas and said any change needs a holistic empirical review.

133.s: Which case held that no data on backwardness is needed for SC/ST reservation in promotion and that the creamy layer applies?
133.x: Jarnail Singh (2018) dropped the need for backwardness data for SC/ST promotion and applied the creamy layer.
133.tq: one-liner

133.s: Which case limited Article 16(4) to initial appointment and set a 50% ceiling on reservation?
133.x: Indra Sawhney (1992) held that 16(4) applies only at initial appointment and fixed the 50% ceiling.
133.tq: one-liner

133.s: The causes of atrocity on Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribes according to the report of National Commission for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe in the year 1990 do not include -
133.x: The National Commission for SCs and STs (1990) listed land disputes and alienation, bonded labour, indebtedness and non-payment of minimum wages as causes of atrocities – not religious causes.

133.s: In which year did the Karamchedu incident take place?
133.x: Karamchedu was in 1985, after the Siddhantam temple entry (1933) and before Tsundur (1991).
xa: Siddhantam was in **Krishna** district.
Tsundur was in **Guntur** district.

133.s: In 2017, for what did the NCRB add a separate crime head for SCs?
o: Being forced to leave residence or facing social boycott
Denial of reservation in educational institutions
133.x: The 2017 NCRB crime head covered persons forced to leave their residence or facing social boycott. Uttar Pradesh recorded 57 cases under this head that year.
133.tq: Recall the exact wording of a newly introduced crime category.
xs: The **2017** NCRB head: SCs **forced to leave residence / facing social boycott** — option **(1)** is correct.
**UP** recorded **57** cases that year.
xa: Dalit labourers depend on dominant-caste landowners and **hide complaints** for fear of boycott.
⚠ **Mysore HC**: social boycott of a few individuals is **not** untouchability under Art. 17.

133.s: Which body's reports list land alienation, bonded labour, indebtedness and non-payment of wages as causes of caste atrocities?
o: National Commission for SCs and STs
133.x: Reports of the National Commission for SCs and STs list these causes; religious causes are not included.

133.s: Caste hierarchy, upper-caste dominance, rising Dalit activism and political interference are factors behind which of the following?
133.x: All four are identified as factors contributing to caste atrocities.
xa: The **1990** Commission listed land alienation, bonded labour, indebtedness, non-payment of wages.
Dalit labourers **hide complaints** for fear of boycott.
**UP** had **57** social-boycott cases in **2017**.

133.s: Karamchedu, Tsundur and Khairlanji are respectively associated with which States?
o: Andhra Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra
Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh
133.x: Karamchedu and Tsundur occurred in Andhra Pradesh, while Khairlanji occurred in Maharashtra.
133.tq: Use location pairing to distinguish closely related atrocity incidents.
xs: **Karamchedu** — AP; **Tsundur** — AP; **Khairlanji** — **Maharashtra**: option **(1)** is correct.
**Karamchedu** (**17 Jul 1985**): then Prakasam, now Bapatla; **Tsundur** (**6 Aug 1991**): Guntur.
**Khairlanji** (**29 Sep 2006**): Bhandara district.
xa: Karamchedu **sparked the independent Dalit movement**.
**Hathras** (**2020**, UP): SC entrusted monitoring to the **Allahabad HC**.

133.s: Karamchedu incident is associated with which one of the following descriptions?
o: It resulted in monitoring by the Allahabad High Court.
It involved four members of a Dalit family in Bhandara district.
It led to the creation of the NCRB crime head for social boycott.
It sparked the independent Dalit movement.
133.x: The Karamchedu incident of 1985, in which Madiga Dalits were killed by dominant-caste landlords, sparked the independent Dalit movement.
133.tq: Identify the distinctive consequence attached to the incident.
xs: **Karamchedu** **sparked the independent Dalit movement** — option **(4)** is correct.
Madiga Dalits were killed by dominant-caste landlords (**17 Jul 1985**).
Allahabad HC monitoring = **Hathras**; Bhandara = **Khairlanji**.
xa: APP gives **1985**; CDX prints **1982**.
Then Prakasam district, now **Bapatla**.

133.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Poona Pact
B. Ambedkar’s declaration at Yeola
C. Karamchedu incident
D. Tsundur incident
133.x: The Poona Pact took place in 1932, the Yeola declaration in 1935, Karamchedu in 1985 and Tsundur in 1991.
133.tq: Fix the earliest two events first, then place the incidents by year.
xs: Correct order is **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**Poona Pact** (**1932**) → **Yeola** declaration (**1935**).
xa: The **Harijan Sevak Sangh** was founded in **1932** after the Poona Pact.
**Khairlanji** (Maharashtra) came in **2006**.
Karamchedu **sparked the independent Dalit movement**.

133.s: In the Hathras case, to whom did the Supreme Court entrust monitoring?
133.x: In the Hathras case, the Supreme Court entrusted monitoring to the Allahabad High Court.
133.tq: Identify the authority entrusted with a specific monitoring responsibility.
xs: In **Hathras** (**2020**, UP), the SC entrusted monitoring to the **Allahabad High Court** — option **(3)** is correct.
The monitoring was not given to the NHRC or any other High Court.
xa: **Khairlanji** (**2006**) = Maharashtra.
**Karamchedu** (**1985**) and **Tsundur** (**1991**) = AP.
NCRB **2017** crime head: social boycott.

133.s: As per NCRB data for 2023, which State recorded the most crimes against Scheduled Castes?
133.x: Uttar Pradesh (15,130) led, followed by Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, out of 57,789 cases.
133.tq: one-liner

133.s: Where did B.R. Ambedkar declare "I was born a Hindu, but I will not die a Hindu"?
133.x: B. R. Ambedkar made this declaration at Yeola in 1935.
133.tq: Discriminate between a leader’s quotation, place and year.
xs: Ambedkar declared "I was born a Hindu... but I will not die a Hindu" at **Yeola** in **1935** — option **(4)** is correct.
It sits with his other stands: caste is "**a division of labourers**" and **Dalit** over 'Harijan'.
xa: He wrote **Annihilation of Caste** in **1936**.
**Kalaram Temple Entry**: **1930**, Nashik.
**Mahad Satyagraha**: **20 Mar 1927**.

133.s: In which period was the Adi-Andhra movement, which claimed Dalits were the original inhabitants of Andhra, mainly active?
133.x: The movement was active in the 1910s–30s and demanded access to education, temples and tanks.
xa: **Siddhantam Temple Entry** (**1933**, Krishna district) was one of the earliest in Andhra.
Andhra Dalit papers: **Adi Andhra** (Didla Pullaiah), **Nava Jeevan** (Undru Subbarao).

133.s: Who criticised the Harijan Sevak Sangh as paternalistic?
133.x: Bhagya Reddy Varma criticised the Harijan Sevak Sangh as paternalistic; Gandhi used the term 'Harijan'.
xa: Ambedkar sought **annihilation of caste**.
Gandhi called untouchability "**a blot on Hinduism**".
**Periyar**: political freedom is meaningless without social equality.

133.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Jagan Mitra Mandali — Bhagya Reddy Varma
Harijan Sevak Sangh — Manda Krishna Madiga
133.x: The Harijan Sevak Sangh was associated with Gandhi, whereas Manda Krishna Madiga led the Madiga Dandora movement.
133.tq: Use a nearby movement leader as the distractor and identify the swapped association.
xs: **Harijan Sevak Sangh — Manda Krishna Madiga** is NOT correct — option **(4)**; the Sangh was **Gandhi**'s (**1932**).
**Manda Krishna Madiga** founded the **MRPS** (**1994**, Madiga Dandora).
The rest are right: **Gabbilam** — Jashuva; **Jagan Mitra Mandali** — Bhagya Reddy Varma; **Safai Karmachari Andolan** — Bezwada Wilson.
xa: MRPS was founded at **Eedumudi**, **Prakasam** district.
Bhagya Reddy Varma criticised the Harijan Sevak Sangh as **paternalistic**.

133.s:
Assertion (A): Ambedkar advocated legal-constitutional rights and the annihilation of caste.
Reason (R): Ambedkar supported reform of caste only from within Hindu society.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
133.x: A is correct; R is false because reform from within is associated with Gandhi, not Ambedkar.
xa: Gandhi relied on **moral persuasion**; founded **Harijan Sevak Sangh** (**1932**).
**Annihilation of Caste** includes a rebuke of Gandhi's approach.

133.s: Which of the following pairs relating to Andhra Dalit newspapers is correct?
133.x: Adi Andhra was associated with Didla Pullaiah, while Nava Jeevan was associated with Undru Subbarao.
133.tq: Discriminate between two similar newspaper–editor associations.
xs: **Adi Andhra** — **Didla Pullaiah** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Nava Jeevan** was by **Undru Subbarao**, not Didla Pullaiah.
xa: The **Adi-Andhra movement** (**1910s-30s**) claimed Dalits were Andhra's original inhabitants.
Gandhi's paper **Harijan** began in **1933**.

133.s: What is the central idea of Gurram Jashuva's Gabbilam?
o: A bat can enter a temple while an untouchable cannot
A king grants land to temple servants
A crow carries a message from Buddha to an emperor
A temple priest abolishes caste through ritual
133.x: In Gabbilam, an untouchable labourer sends his plea to Lord Shiva through a bat because the bat may enter the temple while he may not.
133.tq: Test the central image and social contrast in a literary work.
xs: In **Gabbilam**, a bat may **enter the temple** while the untouchable cannot — option **(1)** is correct.
So the **untouchable labourer** sends his plea to **Lord Shiva** through the bat.
xa: Written by **Gurram Jashuva** in **1941**.
Modelled on **Kalidasa's Meghaduta**.
⚠ **Gabbilam** = bat (**1941**); **Gulamgiri** = slavery (**1873**).

133.s: Which one of the following combinations relating to Vaikom Satyagraha is correct?
o: Travancore — T.K. Madhavan and Keshava Menon — 1924–25
133.x: Vaikom Satyagraha took place in Travancore in 1924–25 and was organised by T.K. Madhavan and Keshava Menon, with K. Kelappan also associated with it.
133.tq: Start with the sure location and verify the corresponding leaders and date.
xs: **Travancore — T.K. Madhavan and Keshava Menon — 1924-25** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Mahad** was Ambedkar's (**1927**); **Nashik** = Kalaram (**1930**); **Krishna district** = Siddhantam (**1933**).
xa: **K. Kelappan** also took part; **Sree Narayana Guru** supported it.
**Periyar** was jailed in it.
⚠ **Mahad** = water (**20 Mar 1927**); **Kalaram** = temple (**1930**).

133.s: Which right of Dalits did B.R. Ambedkar assert through the Mahad Chavdar Tank Satyagraha?
o: Draw water from a public tank
Use roads around the Vaikom temple
133.x: The Mahad Satyagraha, held at Mahad in Maharashtra on 20 March 1927, asserted Dalits’ right to draw water from the public Chavdar Tank.
133.tq: Identify a movement from its precise immediate objective.
xs: **Mahad (Chavdar Tank) Satyagraha** asserted Dalits' right to **draw water from a public tank** — option **(2)** is correct.
Led by **Ambedkar** on **20 Mar 1927** at Mahad (Maharashtra).
xa: **Centenary (2026-27)** began **20 Mar 2026**.
**Manusmriti Dahan**: **25 Dec 1927**.
⚠ **Kalaram** = temple entry (**1930**, Nashik).

133.s: When was the Mahad (Chavdar Tank) Satyagraha led by B.R. Ambedkar held?
133.x: The Mahad Satyagraha was on 20 March 1927 (centenary from 20 March 2026); the Manusmriti Dahan was on 25 December 1927.
xa: ⚠ **Mahad** = water; **Kalaram** = temple.
Ambedkar led **15,000** volunteers at Kalaram.

133.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
133.x: The Siddhantam Temple Entry movement took place in Krishna district in 1933 and was one of the earliest such movements in Andhra. The other options confuse its details with those of other movements.
133.tq: Check location and date together to expose swapped movement details.
xs: **Siddhantam Temple Entry — 1933 — Krishna district** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was led by Congress/Gandhian leaders, one of the **earliest in Andhra**.
**Kalaram** was **1930** at **Nashik**; **Mahad** was **1927** in Maharashtra.
xa: **Vaikom** (**1924-25**) was in Travancore.
AP angle also includes **Jashuva**'s **Gabbilam** and **Jogin** rehabilitation.

133.s: Which of the following pairs (Work – Author) is correctly matched?

135.s: Regarding schedule Caste and schedule tribe reservation choose the correct answer

To encourage emigration to urban areas

136.s: Which of the following is a better way of protecting reserve forests?
o: Keeping them out of bounds for locals
Allowing limited rights like grazing rights to locals
Privatization of forest management through big corporates
136.src: APPSC Civil Assistant Surgeon (Specialist) in AP Vaidya Vidh
136.x: Allowing limited rights such as grazing gives locals a stake in protecting reserve forests; total exclusion, unlimited rights or corporate privatisation do not.

136.s: At the national level, which ministry is the nodal agency to ensure effective implementation of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006?

136.s: Whose decision is final in vesting of the rights under the Scheduled Tribes and other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006?
136.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-II Screening Test 2017
136.x: Under Sec. 6(6) of the FRA the decision of the District Level Committee on the record of forest rights is final and binding; the Gram Sabha only initiates the process.

136.s: The Scheduled Tribes and other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 was passed in India on:
136.x:
Most keys: 18 December 2006 (passed by Parliament). Strictly: Lok Sabha passed it on 15 December and the President assented on 29 December 2006 (ncst.nic.in; India Code).
Parliament completed passage of the Forest Rights Bill on 18 December 2006 (Rajya Sabha; Lok Sabha 15 December); assent came on 29 December 2006. (The printed key was missing.)

136.s: Under the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, who shall be the authority to initiate the process for determining the nature and extent of individual or community forest rights or both?
o: Tahsildar /Block Development Officer / Mandai Revenue Officer
136.x: Under the FRA the Gram Sabha is the competent authority to initiate determination of individual or community forest rights.

136.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The definition of "Critical Wildlife Habitat is incorporated in the Forest Rights Act, of 2006.
2. For the first time in India, Baigas have been given Habitat Rights.
3. Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change officially decides and declares Habitat Rights for Primitive and Vulnerable Tribal Groups in any part of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
136.x: 1 is correct – Critical Wildlife Habitat is defined only in the FRA. 2 is correct – the Baiga of Madhya Pradesh were the first to get habitat rights (2015-16). 3 is wrong – habitat rights are decided under the FRA with MoTA, not MoEFCC. So 1 and 2.

136.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. As per recent amendment to the Indian Forest Act, 1927, forest dwellers have the right to fell the bamboos grown on forest areas.
2. As per the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, bamboo is a minor forest produce.
3. The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 allows ownership of minor forest produce to forest dwellers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
136.x: 1 is wrong – the 2017 IFA amendment removed bamboo grown outside forests from 'tree', giving no right to fell bamboo in forests. 2 and 3 are right – bamboo is MFP under the FRA, which gives forest dwellers ownership of MFP. So 2 and 3 only.

136.s: Under the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, who shall be the authority to initiate the process for determining the nature and extent of individual or community forest rights or both?
136.x: Under Sec. 6(1) of the FRA the Gram Sabha initiates the process of determining individual or community forest rights; the claims then go to the sub-divisional and district committees.

136.s: Why did the Forest Conservation Rules, 2022 become a subject of dispute between the NCST and the Environment Ministry?
o: Added a compulsory tribal veto over every forest diversion
Dropped the forest-dwellers’ consent clause before forest diversion
Prohibited all development projects in forest areas
Transferred all forests to Gram Sabhas
136.x: The 2022 Rules dropped the consent clause of forest-dwellers before forest diversion, leading to a dispute between the NCST and the Environment Ministry.
136.tq: Identify the precise legal change behind an institutional dispute.
xs: The **Forest Conservation Rules 2022** **dropped the forest-dwellers' consent clause** before forest diversion — option **(2)**.
This set the **NCST** against the **Environment Ministry**.
xa: MoEFCC guidelines had barred diversion until FRA processes (esp. **Gram Sabha consent**) were complete.
MoTA letter (**31 Aug 2026**): FRA has **"no provision"** for Gram Sabha consent for **Stage-II** clearance.
**Niyamgiri (2013)**: **Dongria Kondh** gram sabhas rejected bauxite mining → project cancelled.

136.s: Which is the nodal Ministry for implementing the Forest Rights Act, 2006?
o: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
136.x: The Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the nodal ministry for the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
136.tq: Use the who-is-responsible test to distinguish the nodal ministry from ministries involved in implementation.
xs: The **Ministry of Tribal Affairs** is the **nodal ministry** for the **FRA 2006** — option **(1)** (UPSC **2021**).
**MoEFCC** handles forest diversion; it was asked by MoTA for **CFR funds** (**12 Jan 2026**).
xa: FRA aims to undo the "**historical injustice**" and **overrides** inconsistent laws.
MoTA letter (**31 Aug 2026**): FRA has "no provision" for Gram Sabha consent for **Stage-II** clearance.
MoTA was set up in **1999**.

136.s: Under the Forest Rights Act, each Sub-Divisional and District Level Committee has how many members?
136.x: The Sub-Divisional and District Level Committees are six-member bodies of revenue, tribal and forest officials and elected panchayat members.

136.s: Which of the following is NOT recognised as a forest right under the Forest Rights Act, 2006?
o: Automatic ownership of all mineral resources beneath forest land
Habitat rights for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups
136.x: The Act recognises rights such as minor forest produce, community forest resource management and PVTG habitat rights. It does not confer automatic ownership of all mineral resources beneath forest land.
136.tq: Find the option outside the statutory list of individual and community forest rights.
xs: NOT an FRA right: **automatic ownership of all mineral resources** beneath forest land — option **(1)**.
FRA rights list: **ownership of MFP**, **habitat rights for PVTGs**, **community forest resources** management, biodiversity/traditional knowledge.
xa: Individual rights: land, **habitation**, **self-cultivation**.
Community rights: **nistar**, **grazing**, fishing, **CFR** management.
⚠ **Samatha (1997)**: mining leases in Scheduled Areas to private non-tribals are **void**.

136.s: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 sought to undo the historical injustice done to whom?
136.x: The Act recognises forest rights of Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers, with the stated objective of undoing historical injustice to forest dwellers.
xa: Nodal ministry: **Tribal Affairs** (UPSC **2021**).
The Act **overrides** inconsistent laws.
Beneficiaries: **FDST** and **OTFD**.

136.s: A forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribe family claims recognition of rights under the Forest Rights Act. Which date is relevant for determining occupation of forest land?
136.x: Forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes must have been occupying the forest land before 13 December 2005 for eligibility under the stated cut-off criterion.
136.tq: Treat the cut-off date as a direct numerical-recall point and reject nearby constitutional or enactment dates.
xs: The cut-off for FDSTs is occupation **before 13 December 2005** — option **(3)**.
FDSTs must be **living in, dependent on and occupying** forest land before that date.
xa: **OTFDs** need **3 generations (75 years)** of residence before **2005**.
Ceiling: up to **4 ha** per family.
Claims start with the **Gram Sabha** (**Sec. 6**).

136.s: For how long must Other Traditional Forest Dwellers show residence in or dependence on forests for recognition under the Forest Rights Act?
136.x: Other Traditional Forest Dwellers must show residence in or dependence on forests for three generations, specified as 75 years, before 2005.
136.tq: Separate the generation requirement from the ST cut-off date and convert it into the stated year equivalent.
xs: OTFDs need **three generations or 75 years** — option **(3)**.
FDSTs instead need occupation **before 13 December 2005**.
xa: OTFD = **Other Traditional Forest Dwellers**; FDST = **Forest-dwelling STs**.
Ceiling: up to **4 hectares per family**.
Committees: **six-member** Sub-Divisional and District Level Committees.

136.s: What is the maximum extent of forest rights that may be recognised per family under the Forest Rights Act, 2006?
136.x: The ceiling for forest rights is up to four hectares per family.
136.tq: Test the statutory ceiling directly using close numerical distractors.
xs: The FRA ceiling is up to **4 hectares** per family — option **(1)**.
For public utilities (schools, dispensaries), diversion is up to **1 ha per project** on **Gram Sabha** recommendation.
xa: Individual rights: land, habitation, self-cultivation.
Titles (**2025-26**): **23.92 lakh individual + 1.22 lakh community**.
AP: **2,26,651** individual titles approved (APSES **2024-25**).

136.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with an individual forest right rather than a community forest right?
136.x: Habitation and self-cultivation are individual rights. Nistar, grazing, fishing and community forest resource management are examples of community rights.
136.tq: Separate individual and community rights by identifying the beneficiary and nature of use.
xs: **Habitation and self-cultivation** are **individual** rights — option **(1)**.
**Grazing**, **fishing** and **CFR management** are **community** rights.
xa: Community rights also include **nistar**.
Other rights: **ownership of MFP**, **habitat rights for PVTGs**.
⚠ Implementation gap: focus on **individual titles over CFR**.

136.s: What is the position of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 in relation to laws inconsistent with it?
o: Applies only where no State law exists
Can be overridden by an executive circular
136.x: The Forest Rights Act overrides laws that are inconsistent with its provisions.

136.s: Which Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group was the first to receive habitat rights under the Forest Rights Act?
136.x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (Baiga of Madhya Pradesh); it is added as option 5.
The first habitat rights in India went to the Baiga of Baigachak (Dindori, Madhya Pradesh) in 2015-16; the Bharia of Patalkot (MP) got them only in 2022 and the Baiga and Kamar of Chhattisgarh later, so the old key 'Bharia' was wrong and no printed option is correct.
136.tq: Use the first-in-sequence trap to distinguish Bharia from the later Kamar and Baiga claims.

136.s: Under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, what type of right is 'nistar'?
136.x: Nistar, grazing, fishing and ownership and disposal of minor forest produce are listed community rights under the FRA.
xa: **Bamboo** is an MFP under the FRA (UPSC **2019**).
**Nistar** = a community right.
**TRIFED** gives **MSP for MFP**.

136.s: What is to be done with areas of national parks and sanctuaries declared Critical Wildlife Habitat under the Forest Rights Act?
o: Transferred exclusively to private conservation agencies
Kept inviolate after an open process involving affected communities
Opened for mining after approval by the Forest Department
136.x: Critical Wildlife Habitats are areas within national parks and sanctuaries to be kept inviolate, and they are notified after an open process with affected communities.
136.tq: Distinguish the legal definition from an assumed blanket exclusion of communities.
xs: **Critical Wildlife Habitats** are areas of national parks/sanctuaries **kept inviolate** after an **open process with affected communities** — option **(3)**.
They are defined and notified under the **FRA** (UPSC **2018**).
xa: ⚠ **Critical tiger habitats** (WPA) need **mandatory Gram Sabha consultation**.
**Agasthyamalai**: eviction orders ignored the FRA (**11 Aug 2026**).
The FRA overrides inconsistent laws.

136.s: The Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 did which of the following?
o: Removed bamboo grown outside forest areas from the definition of “tree”.
Granted an unrestricted right to fell bamboo in forest areas.
Removed all bamboo from the definition of minor forest produce.
Transferred ownership of all bamboo to private companies.
136.x: The 2017 amendment removed bamboo grown outside forest areas from the definition of “tree”. It did not confer a right to fell bamboo in forest areas.
136.tq: Watch for the false extension from bamboo outside forests to bamboo inside forests.
xs: **IFA (Amendment) 2017** **removed bamboo grown outside forest areas** from the definition of "**tree**" — option **(1)**.
⚠ It did **not** give a right to fell bamboo in forest areas — that comes from the **FRA**.
xa: Under the FRA, **bamboo is MFP**, owned by forest dwellers.
UPSC **2019**: statement on IFA right to fell = false.
**PM Janjatiya Vikas Mission** buys MFP at **MSP**.

136.s: Which one of the following statements regarding bamboo under the Forest Rights Act is correct?
o: Bamboo is a tree in every location and cannot be collected by forest dwellers.
Bamboo is a minor forest produce, and ownership is vested in forest dwellers.
Bamboo is excluded from minor forest produce and belongs only to the Forest Department.
Ownership of bamboo is vested only in Gram Panchayats.
136.x: The Forest Rights Act treats bamboo as a minor forest produce and vests its ownership in forest dwellers.
136.tq: Separate the FRA status of bamboo from its treatment under the Indian Forest Act amendment.
xs: **Bamboo is a minor forest produce** under the FRA, with **ownership vested in forest dwellers** — option **(2)**.
UPSC **2019** key: this was the correct statement.
xa: **IFA (Amendment) 2017** removed bamboo grown **outside forest areas** from "tree".
⚠ IFA 2017 did **not** give a right to fell bamboo in forest areas.
**TRIFED** gives **MSP for MFP**.

136.s: Which of the following is NOT a reported gap in Forest Rights Act implementation?

o: Required only for private projects and never for public projects
Replaced by a census of affected families

It is not optional in Scheduled Areas — there it applies along with **Gram Sabha** consent.
xa: Consent: **80% (private)**, **70% (PPP)** affected families.

o: Only the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes
Gram Sabha, Panchayat or Autonomous Council, as applicable

xs: In Scheduled Areas, acquisition is a **last resort** and needs **Gram Sabha/Panchayat/Autonomous Council consent** — option **(4)**.

**PESA** areas: at least **50%** seats to STs and **all chairpersons are STs**.

136.s: Which of the following is NOT correct regarding forest diversion and the Forest Rights Act?
o: MoEF's 2009 circular required completion of FRA processes before forest diversion under the FCA
Under the 2009 circular, forest diversion could go ahead before FRA claims were settled if the project was of public importance

136.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the process of declaring Scheduled Tribes in India:

1. The President can, by public notification, declare any tribe as a Scheduled Tribe only after consultation with the Governor.

2. The President can modify the list of Scheduled Tribes from time to time based on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

3. Only Parliament has the power to make changes to the list of Scheduled Tribes.

4. Once a tribe gets Scheduled status, all its members across the nation automatically receive the benefits of this status.
Which of the above statements are correct?
136.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer (A.P. Tribal Welfare
136.x: 1 is right – the President notifies STs after consulting the Governor (Art. 342(1)); 3 is right – later changes only by Parliament by law (Art. 342(2)). 2 is wrong (the President cannot modify the list later) and 4 is wrong (ST status is State/UT-specific). So 1 and 3 only.

B. Bihar

C. Chhattisgarh

E. Karnataka
Choose the correct answer:

136.s:
The specifications required for a community to be declared as a Scheduled Tribe are :
1. Indications of primitive traits
2. Sistinctive culture
3. Shyness of contact with the community at large
4. Backwardness and geographical isolation
Which of the above are correct?
136.x: The criteria for specifying a Scheduled Tribe are primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact with the community at large and backwardness – all four listed.

136.s: Scheduled Tribe status is –
136.x: Scheduled Tribe status is religiously neutral – a member of any religion can be an ST, while SC status is limited to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists.

136.s: The term 'Scheduled Tribes' is defined in which provision of the Constitution of India?
136.x: Article 366(25) defines Scheduled Tribes. Article 342(2) lets Parliament modify the ST list, Article 338A creates the NCST, and Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to Scheduled Areas.
136.tq: Definition = 366(25); list change by Parliament = 342(2).
xs: Scheduled Tribes are defined in **Article 366(25)** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 342(2)**: Parliament modifies the **ST list**; **Art. 338A**: the **NCST**.
xa: ST inclusion: State → **Registrar General of India** → NCST → Cabinet → Parliament.
The **Fifth Schedule** and **Art. 244** protect Scheduled Areas (cited in the **Parasnath Hills** debate).
ST status is **religiously neutral** (RPSC **2010**).

137.s: What did the Supreme Court recognise for children below 14 years in Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)?
o: A right to employment in non-hazardous industries
A statutory right to adoption under Article 24
A fundamental duty to provide education under Article 51A(k)
A fundamental right to free education under Article 21
